topics.ch: Indian Society: Introducing Indian Society
topics.h: You already 'know' Indian society: you have lived in it for 17 years. Sociology's first surprise is that this knowledge can be the very thing that stops you from seeing clearly.
p: This introductory chapter is non-evaluative in the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus, but its ideas run through the whole book.
Common-sense knowledge comes from socialisation: family, neighbourhood, school and media teach us what is 'normal'. It is real knowledge, but often partial and taken for granted.
Sociology asks us to unlearn: to set aside taken-for-granted ideas and look at familiar things as if seeing them for the first time.
Self-reflexivity is the ability to look at ourselves from the outside, as others might see us, and to question our own position and assumptions.

Sociology works like a social map: it shows where an individual stands in the wider landscape of groups, institutions and history. The book then covers demography, caste, tribe and family, inequality, cultural diversity and project work.

ex.q: Meera, from a city family, says 'Everyone eats three meals at a table.' How would a self-reflexive sociologist respond?
st: Notice that this is a common-sense belief learnt through her own socialisation.
Ask whose experience it reflects: her class, region and urban location.
Compare with other groups: farm workers, migrants, hostel students, families that sit on the floor.
Revise the claim after seeing her own position on the 'social map'.
ex.a: She treats her habit as one position among many, not as a universal fact. That is self-reflexivity.

topics.rl: A Delhi student on an NSS camp in rural Odisha notices that 'normal' timings for meals, work and school are very different there. Questioning her own idea of 'normal' is the first step of sociology.

rv.summary: Our common-sense knowledge of society comes from socialisation and is often partial. Sociology asks us to unlearn taken-for-granted ideas and practise self-reflexivity, seeing our own place on the 'social map'.

What unlearning and self-reflexivity mean, and why they matter most when studying one's own society
The 'social map' idea: locating a person within the wider society and its history

This introductory chapter is non-evaluative in the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus
traps: Unlearning does not mean rejecting all prior knowledge; it means questioning what we take for granted
Don't read 'social map' literally as geography; it shows our place in society
Don't think reflexivity is only for unfamiliar cultures; familiarity makes our own biases harder to see

topics.ch: Indian Society: Introducing Indian Society
topics.t: Colonialism and the making of modern India
topics.h: The train you take to your nani's house runs on tracks first laid for carrying cotton and coal to the ports. Colonialism built modern India, but for its own purposes.
p: Modern Indian society, and Indians' awareness of themselves as a society, took shape in the context of colonial rule.
Colonialism unified India administratively and economically for the first time in a modern way, but this unification came through exploitation and domination.
Key colonial changes: railways and telegraph, a uniform legal and court system, new land revenue settlements, modern English education and a centralised bureaucracy.
The paradox of colonialism: it produced the very forces that opposed it. Western-educated Indians used ideas of liberty, rights and nationhood against British rule.
So colonialism was both a unifying and a dividing, both a modernising and an exploiting force.

ex.q: How did railways show the double face of colonialism?
st: Purpose: railways moved raw materials to ports and British goods inland, and helped move troops.
Effect: they also connected regions, allowed travel, pilgrimage and the spread of newspapers and ideas.
Result: Indians from distant regions could meet and organise, which helped nationalism.
ex.a: Built for colonial profit and control, railways also helped Indians see themselves as one people.

topics.rl: Indian Railways still uses many 19th-century routes; today they carry crores of passengers, but their original map was drawn around colonial ports such as Bombay, Calcutta and Madras.

rv.summary: Modern Indian society and Indians' self-awareness took shape under colonial rule. Colonialism unified India administratively and economically, but through exploitation, and it also produced the forces that opposed it.

Colonialism as both unifying and dividing, modernising and exploiting

Colonial unification was real, but achieved through exploitation and domination
traps: Don't confuse an unintended effect with the purpose: railways helped nationalism but were built for colonial profit and control
Don't treat colonial unification as either fully good or not real
Don't think the past has no bearing on the present; many present institutions took shape under colonialism

topics.ch: Indian Society: Introducing Indian Society
topics.h: In 1885 a few dozen delegates met in Bombay; within decades, peasants, workers, students and women across the subcontinent were marching. How did so many different people come to feel like one nation?
p: Indian nationalism grew through the anti-colonial struggle; the shared experience of colonial domination helped people imagine India as one nation.
Under colonialism, communities based on caste, tribe, religion and region began to organise themselves in new ways, through associations, petitions and newspapers.
New classes emerged: an urban middle class of professionals, industrial workers, and peasants facing new revenue demands. Each organised around its own interests.
Reform movements (for example against sati or for women's education) and revival movements reshaped how communities saw themselves.
So nationalism coexisted with, and was shaped by, community and class identities, sometimes in harmony and sometimes in tension.

ex.q: Give two kinds of identity, other than nation, that became organised in colonial India, with one example each.
st: Community identity: caste associations petitioning for recognition, or religious reform bodies.
Class identity: industrial workers forming trade unions, or peasants protesting revenue demands.
Both used modern means such as print, meetings and petitions.
ex.a: Community (caste, tribe, religion, region) and class (middle class, workers, peasants) identities both organised.

topics.rl: When you see a caste association's hall, a trade union office and a regional language newspaper in the same town today, you are seeing three kinds of collective identity that took modern shape in colonial times.

rv.summary: Indian nationalism grew through the shared struggle against colonial rule. At the same time, communities (caste, tribe, religion, region) and new classes organised in modern ways, sometimes in harmony and sometimes in tension with nationalism.

New means of organising: associations, petitions, newspapers and public meetings
Role of reform and revival movements in reshaping how communities saw themselves
remember: Nationalism coexisted with, and was shaped by, community and class identities
The new middle class: Western-educated lawyers, teachers and clerks created by colonial education
traps: Don't confuse class with community: industrial workers and peasants protesting revenue are class-based
Don't assume unity meant no tension; groups also pursued their own interests
Don't confuse the new middle class with landed elites

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.t: What demography studies, and the census
topics.h: Every ten years, lakhs of enumerators knock on every door in India, from Ladakh to Lakshadweep, and ask the same questions. That giant headcount is the raw material of demography.
p: Demography is the systematic study of population: its size, composition (age, sex, literacy and so on), distribution over space, and change over time.

Formal demography is mathematical; it measures and forecasts population numbers. Social demography (population studies) looks at the social, economic and political causes and effects of population trends.
Demography grew alongside the modern nation-state and the science of statistics, because states wanted to count, plan for and govern their people. The census is its key data source.
In India, the first census attempts were made between 1867 and 1872; a regular census has been held every ten years since 1881. Independent India continued this decennial census from 1951.
Durkheim showed that suicide rates differ steadily between groups. Rates are therefore social facts: they reveal social patterns that individual stories cannot.

ex.q: A researcher calculates that a district's population grew by 18 per cent in a decade; another asks why families there prefer sons. Which kind of demography is each doing?
st: Calculating growth is measurement and counting.
So the first researcher is doing formal demography.
Asking about son preference looks at social causes and effects.
So the second researcher is doing social demography.
ex.a: First: formal demography. Second: social demography (population studies).

topics.rl: Planning how many AIIMS-type hospitals, Kendriya Vidyalayas or ration shops a district needs starts with census figures on its population, age and literacy.

rv.summary: Demography is the systematic study of a population's size, composition, distribution and change. It has a mathematical branch (formal demography) and a social branch (social demography), and the census is its key data source.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.h: In 1798 an English clergyman predicted that humanity would always outrun its food. More than two centuries later, the world has more people than ever, and far more food. What did Malthus miss?
p: Thomas Robert Malthus argued that population grows in a geometric progression (2, 4, 8, 16...) while food supply grows only in an arithmetic progression (1, 2, 3, 4...).
So population would always press on food, keeping most people near subsistence. Prosperity could only be secured by controlling population growth.
Positive checks are natural ones that raise deaths: famines, diseases and wars. Preventive checks are human choices that lower births: late marriage, celibacy and sexual abstinence.

Criticisms: European history showed population and living standards both rising; technology greatly raised food output. Liberal and Marxist scholars argued poverty comes from unequal distribution of resources, not from population itself.

ex.q: Starting with population 2 units and food 1 unit, and doubling population while food rises by 1 unit each period, what are the values after three more periods?
st: Population: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 (geometric).
Food: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 (arithmetic).
Population per unit of food: 16 / 4 = 4, up from 2.
ex.a: Population 16, food 4: the gap widens, which is Malthus's warning.

topics.rl: India went from food imports in the 1960s to large grain buffer stocks in FCI godowns after the Green Revolution, even as population kept rising, a real-life challenge to Malthus.

rv.summary: Malthus argued that population grows geometrically while food grows only arithmetically, so population controls were needed for prosperity. Critics pointed to rising living standards, technology and unequal distribution of resources.

Positive checks versus preventive checks, with examples
The main criticisms: European history, technology, and the liberal and Marxist view of distribution

traps: Don't swap the two progressions: population is geometric, food is arithmetic
'Positive' check does not mean a good, voluntary check; it means natural checks that raise deaths
Don't add a fixed amount for geometric growth; doubling three times multiplies by 8

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.h: Imagine a village where vaccines arrive overnight but ideas about family size change only over decades. Births stay high, deaths crash, and the population shoots up. That gap is the heart of demographic transition.
p: The theory of demographic transition links population growth to the overall level of economic development. Each society passes through typical stages.
Stage 1: underdeveloped, technologically backward society; high birth rate and high death rate, so slow growth.
Stage 2 (transition): death rate falls sharply with better medicine, food and sanitation, but birth rate stays high. The result is very rapid growth, the 'population explosion'.
Stage 3: developed society; low birth rate and low death rate, so slow growth again.
Why the lag? Death rates can be brought down quickly by technology (vaccines, clean water), while birth rates depend on deep socio-cultural norms about marriage and family that change slowly.

ex.q: A country has birth rate 40 and death rate 38 per 1000. Twenty years later birth rate is 38 and death rate is 15. Which stages are these and what happened?
st: First period: both high, natural increase 40 − 38 = 2 per 1000: Stage 1.
Later: death rate fell sharply, birth rate barely moved; natural increase 38 − 15 = 23 per 1000.
Rapid growth with falling deaths and high births is Stage 2, the transition.
ex.a: It moved from Stage 1 to Stage 2: a population explosion caused by falling mortality.

topics.rl: India's population explosion between 1951 and 1981 followed exactly this pattern: malaria and smallpox control cut deaths quickly, while birth rates fell much more slowly.

rv.summary: The theory of demographic transition links population growth to economic development in three stages. Growth is slow in Stages 1 and 3 but explodes in the transitional stage, when death rates fall fast and birth rates stay high.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.h: If a city of 20 lakh records 44,000 births in a year, is that a lot? Demographers turn raw counts into rates so we can compare Kerala with Bihar or 1951 with 2011.
p: Birth rate (crude birth rate): number of live births per 1000 population in a given area in a year. Death rate: number of deaths per 1000 population per year.
Rate of natural increase (growth rate) = birth rate − death rate (ignoring migration). When it is close to zero, the population has reached replacement level.
Fertility rate: number of live births per 1000 women in the child-bearing age group, usually 15 to 49 years.
Total fertility rate (TFR): the average number of children a woman would bear over her lifetime if she followed current age-specific fertility rates.
Replacement-level TFR is about 2.1 children per woman; the extra 0.1 allows for children who die before reaching reproductive age.

ex.q: A town of 2,00,000 people records 4,800 live births and 1,400 deaths in a year. Find the birth rate, death rate and rate of natural increase.
st: Natural increase = 24 − 7 = 17 per 1000, i.e. 1.7 per cent.
ex.a: Birth rate 24, death rate 7, natural increase 17 per 1000.

topics.rl: Health officers in Kerala and Uttar Pradesh compare TFRs from the Sample Registration System to decide where to focus family-welfare camps and ASHA workers.

rv.summary: Birth and death rates are counted per 1000 population per year, and their difference is the rate of natural increase. Fertility rate uses women aged 15-49 as the base, and replacement-level TFR is about 2.1.

Fertility rate versus crude birth rate: the base used
Meaning of TFR and replacement level

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.t: Infant and maternal mortality, life expectancy and sex ratio
topics.h: A falling infant mortality rate is one of the most sensitive signs of a nation's health. It reflects mothers' nutrition, clean water, vaccines and the reach of public health centres.
p: Infant mortality rate (IMR): number of deaths of babies before the age of one year per 1000 live births.
Maternal mortality rate (MMR): number of women who die in childbirth per 1,00,000 live births.
Low IMR and MMR indicate good health care, nutrition and economic development.
Life expectancy: the estimated number of years an average person is expected to survive, based on age-specific death rates. It rises as health and living conditions improve.
Sex ratio: number of females per 1000 males in a given area at a given time (India's convention). Below 1000 means fewer females than males.

ex.q: In a state, 80,000 live births took place in a year; 2,400 babies died before their first birthday and 96 mothers died in childbirth. Find IMR and MMR.
st: IMR = 2400 / 80000 × 1000 = 30 per 1000 live births.
ex.a: IMR = 30; MMR = 120.

topics.rl: Institutional deliveries under Janani Suraksha Yojana and immunisation drives have helped reduce India's IMR and MMR, especially in rural districts.

rv.summary: IMR counts infant deaths per 1000 live births and MMR counts maternal deaths per 1,00,000 live births; low values signal good health care and development. India's sex ratio is females per 1000 males.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.t: Age structure, dependency and the demographic dividend
topics.h: India is one of the youngest large countries in the world. Crores of young people could power its startups and factories, or swell the queues at employment exchanges. Which one happens depends on choices made now.
p: Age structure is the proportion of people in different age groups. An age pyramid shows it: a wide base means many children; a narrow base and wider top mean an ageing population.
Dependency ratio = (population below 15 + population above 64) ÷ population aged 15-64, often × 100. A falling ratio means relatively more working-age people.
Demographic dividend: the economic advantage of a large working-age share. It is gained only if the young get education, skills and jobs; otherwise it becomes a burden of youth unemployment.
In India, the 0-14 share has been falling and the 15-59 share rising; the 60+ share is slowly growing. Kerala's pyramid is older (more aged people), Uttar Pradesh's is younger (more children).
Population momentum: even after fertility falls, population keeps growing for decades because large young cohorts are entering child-bearing ages.

ex.q: A region has 3,000 children under 15, 600 people over 64 and 6,000 people aged 15-64. Find the dependency ratio.
st: Dependants = 3000 + 600 = 3600.
Working-age = 6000.
Dependency ratio = 3600 / 6000 × 100 = 60.
ex.a: 60 dependants per 100 working-age people.

topics.rl: Skill India and the many engineering, ITI and nursing institutes are attempts to turn India's large youth population into a demographic dividend rather than a jobless crowd.

rv.summary: Age structure, shown by an age pyramid, tells us the share of children, working-age people and the elderly. A large working-age share can give a demographic dividend only if the young get education, skills and jobs.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.t: India's population growth and the fall in death rates
topics.h: Between 1911 and 1921, India's population actually shrank. Between 1951 and 1981 it grew faster than ever before. The story behind these two decades is a story of epidemics, famines and medicine.
p: India's population grew from about 23.8 crore in 1901 to about 121 crore in 2011. Growth was slow until 1921.
1911-21 saw negative growth, mainly because the influenza epidemic of 1918-19 killed millions.
After 1921, and especially in 1951-81, growth was rapid (over 2 per cent a year at its peak) because the death rate fell sharply while the birth rate stayed high.
Death rates fell through control of famines and of epidemic diseases such as plague, smallpox and cholera, plus vaccination, better sanitation and medical care.

Amartya Sen showed famines are caused by a 'failure of entitlements': people lack the means to buy food, not only because food is scarce. Poverty, poor transport and state inaction worsened famines; employment schemes such as MGNREGA (2005) aim to protect rural livelihoods.

ex.q: A table shows India's annual growth rate: 1901-11: 0.56%, 1911-21: −0.03%, 1951-61: 1.96%, 1961-71: 2.20%. What conclusions follow?
st: 1911-21 is negative: population actually fell (influenza epidemic).
Growth jumped after independence, above 2 per cent in 1961-71.
The jump reflects falling death rates while birth rates stayed high.
ex.a: Growth was slow and briefly negative early on, then rose sharply after 1951 as mortality fell.

topics.rl: The smallpox eradication campaign and the near-elimination of famine deaths after 1947 are big reasons India's population grew so fast in the mid-20th century.

rv.summary: India's population grew from about 23.8 crore in 1901 to about 121 crore in 2011, with negative growth in 1911-21 and rapid growth in 1951-81 as death rates fell. Amartya Sen explained famines as a failure of entitlements.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.t: Why birth rates fall slowly: regional fertility differences
topics.h: Kerala and Tamil Nadu reached replacement fertility while some northern states still had TFRs well above 3. Same country, same national policy. Why such different results?
p: Birth rates fall slowly because fertility is a socio-cultural matter: age at marriage, value of children for labour and old-age support, son preference and women's status all play a role.
Falling death rates can come quickly through technology, but family-size norms change over generations.
States like Kerala and Tamil Nadu reached replacement-level fertility; others such as Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Karnataka are close to it.
States like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan have had higher TFRs, so they will account for a large share of India's future growth.
Low fertility usually goes with high female literacy, better health care, later marriage and women's greater say in decisions.

ex.q: Why might a state with high female literacy have lower fertility?
st: Educated women tend to marry later.
They are more aware of contraception and health care, and child survival is higher.
They have more say in family decisions and more work outside the home.
ex.a: Female education delays marriage, improves child survival and empowers women, all of which lower fertility.

topics.rl: ASHA workers in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh focus on delaying marriage and spacing births, the same social changes that earlier lowered fertility in Kerala.

rv.summary: Birth rates fall slowly because fertility depends on social and cultural factors such as age at marriage, son preference and women's status. Kerala and Tamil Nadu reached replacement-level fertility, while states like Bihar and Uttar Pradesh have had higher TFRs.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.h: Biology alone would give slightly more girls than boys in a healthy population, because women tend to live longer. Yet India's sex ratio fell for most of the 20th century. Something social is going on.
p: India's sex ratio declined through the 20th century: about 972 females per 1000 males in 1901 to 927 in 1991, with a small recovery to 933 in 2001.
The child sex ratio (age 0-6) has fallen faster: from 945 in 1991 to 927 in 2001, and lower still in 2011. This points to bias at birth and in early childhood.
Reasons: son preference, neglect of girl children (in food and medical care), female infanticide, and sex-selective abortion made possible by ultrasound technology.
The lowest child sex ratios are found in prosperous regions such as Punjab, Haryana and Delhi, showing that prosperity alone does not remove bias; it can even fund sex selection.
The PNDT Act of 1994 (amended in 2003 as the PCPNDT Act) bans sex determination; Beti Bachao Beti Padhao promotes the value of daughters. Laws help, but lasting change needs changed social attitudes.

ex.q: A district's child sex ratio is 850 while its overall sex ratio is 930. What does this gap suggest?
st: The child ratio covers only ages 0-6, i.e. recent births.
A much lower child ratio means fewer girls are being born or surviving in recent years.
That points to sex-selective abortion or neglect of girl infants.
ex.a: Bias against girls has worsened recently, concentrated at birth and early childhood.

topics.rl: Many districts in Haryana improved their child sex ratio after strict PCPNDT enforcement and Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaigns, though change in attitudes remains the real goal.

rv.summary: India's sex ratio declined through the 20th century, and the child sex ratio has fallen even faster, pointing to bias against girls at birth and in early childhood. Laws like the PCPNDT Act help, but lasting change needs changed social attitudes.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.h: In 1951 fewer than one in five Indians could read; by 2011 about three in four could. Meanwhile crores of people moved from village to city, some for wages, some to escape caste oppression.
p: Literacy empowers people: it opens jobs, awareness and choices, and it is linked to better health and lower fertility, especially female literacy.
Literacy rose from about 18 per cent in 1951 to about 74 per cent in 2011, but a gender gap remains: female literacy is well below male literacy.
Literacy varies by region (Kerala very high, Bihar much lower) and by social group (Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes have lower literacy, especially among women).
About two-thirds of Indians (nearly 69 per cent in 2011) still live in villages, but the urban share is rising. Agriculture's share in GDP has fallen sharply, though many people still depend on it.

Push factors: lack of rural work, decline of common property resources (ponds, forests, grazing lands), and the need for cash. Pull factors: urban jobs and anonymity, which can free lower castes from rural caste oppression. Mass media also carries urban lifestyles into villages.

ex.q: Classify the reasons for Ramesh's move from his village to Surat: (a) his village pond and grazing land were taken over; (b) Surat's textile mills offer wages; (c) in the city nobody asks his caste.
st: (a) Decline of common property resources is a push factor.
(b) Urban jobs are a pull factor.
(c) Anonymity of city life is a pull factor.
ex.a: (a) push; (b) and (c) pull.

topics.rl: Construction sites in Bengaluru and Mumbai are full of migrants from Odisha, Bihar and Jharkhand, pushed by lack of farm work and pulled by daily wages.

rv.summary: Literacy rose from about 18 per cent in 1951 to about 74 per cent in 2011, but gaps remain by gender, region and social group. Most Indians still live in villages, and push and pull factors drive rural-urban migration.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
topics.h: India launched a national family planning programme in 1952, among the first countries in the world to do so. Its journey, including one dark chapter, shows what states can and cannot do about population.
p: The National Family Planning Programme began in 1952. Its objective was to influence the rate and pattern of population growth in socially desirable directions.
Methods included birth control (contraception and sterilisation), improving public health and spreading awareness.
During the Emergency (1975-76) the programme turned coercive: mass sterilisation drives with targets, often forced on poor men, caused a strong public backlash.
After the Emergency it was renamed the National Family Welfare Programme, with a non-coercive approach linking population to maternal and child health and wider welfare.

The National Population Policy 2000 and the National Health Policy 2017 set goals such as reaching replacement-level TFR (2.1) and lowering infant and maternal mortality. The lesson: the state can create conditions, but fertility falls with social and economic change.

st: Targets led officials to force sterilisation on poor and vulnerable people.
This violated consent and created fear and anger.
Public backlash made family planning politically unpopular for years.

topics.rl: Today's health and family-welfare schemes stress choice: spacing methods, counselling by ASHAs and maternal health care, rather than targets.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.t: Caste: varna, jati and its features
topics.h: Caste, tribe and family are institutions you were born into without being asked. This chapter shows how each has stayed the same in some ways and changed in others. We begin with caste, a word that is not even Indian in origin.
p: Caste, tribe and family are key institutions of Indian society; each shows both continuity and change.
The English word 'caste' comes from the Portuguese 'casta' (pure breed). It is used for two Indian terms: varna and jati.
Varna (literally 'colour') is the fourfold all-India classification: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra, with a large group outside it, the 'outcastes' or untouchables (ati-shudra).
Jati is a generic term for species or kinds; jatis are local, regionally variable groups and are the real working units of caste. There are thousands of them.

Features: membership by birth; endogamy (marriage within the group); rules about food and sharing food; a hierarchy of rank; segmental sub-divisions (sub-castes); traditional link with hereditary occupations. Caste was less rigid in the early Vedic period and became rigid later.

ex.q: A woman cannot change her jati by moving to another town, earning more or marrying outside. Which features of caste does this show?
st: She was assigned her caste at birth: membership by birth.
Marriage is expected within the group: endogamy.
Earnings do not change caste rank: caste is ascribed, not achieved.
ex.a: Ascription by birth and endogamy, the two core features.

topics.rl: Matrimonial columns that still specify caste show how endogamy, one of caste's oldest features, continues even in tech-savvy apps and newspapers.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.t: Separation and hierarchy: caste's two principles
topics.h: Caste works like two rules running at once: keep groups apart, and arrange them in a ladder. Together they create a system that is both divided and whole.
p: Principle 1, difference and separation: each caste is supposed to be different from and separate from others, through rules on marriage, food, social interaction and occupation.
Principle 2, wholeness and hierarchy: the separated castes are not equal; they fit into a hierarchical whole, like parts of a body, each with its place.
The hierarchy is based on the distinction between 'purity' and 'pollution': castes considered ritually pure are ranked higher, those considered impure lower.
In theory ritual status and material (economic, political) status could be separate. In practice they usually coincided: upper castes tended to hold land and power, lower castes tended to be poor.

ex.q: Explain how rules about who may cook for whom express both principles of caste.
st: Separation: castes keep apart by not sharing cooked food freely.
Hierarchy: food usually flows from higher to lower, not the reverse, because of purity rules.
So one practice both divides groups and ranks them.
ex.a: Food rules separate castes and rank them by purity and pollution.

topics.rl: Practices like separate utensils for some guests, still reported in surveys in parts of India, show how ideas of purity and pollution can linger in daily life.

rv.summary: Caste works on two principles: difference and separation, and wholeness and hierarchy. The hierarchy rests on purity and pollution, and in practice ritual status and economic status usually coincided.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.h: When British officials tried to count and rank every caste in the 1901 census, thousands of petitions arrived demanding a higher place. Counting caste changed caste.
p: Colonial rulers tried to understand Indian society in order to govern it. Systematic enumeration of caste began with the census.

The 1901 census, under Herbert Risley, tried to collect information on the social hierarchy of castes, i.e. their order of social precedence in each region. This made caste identities more rigid and sparked petitions from castes claiming higher status.
Colonial land revenue settlements and related laws gave legal recognition to the customary rights of upper castes, turning them into owners of land in the modern sense.

The Government of India Act, 1935 gave legal recognition to lists or 'schedules' of castes and tribes marked out for special treatment by the state, origin of the terms Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
So colonialism did not invent caste, but it changed it, making it more rigid and more a matter of official identity.

ex.q: How did the act of counting caste in the census change caste itself?
st: The census asked people to fit into fixed, named caste categories.
In 1901 it also tried to rank castes in a hierarchy.
Castes organised and petitioned for higher rank.
Caste became more rigid and politically important.
ex.a: Official counting froze fluid identities and made caste a matter of state record and competition.

topics.rl: When state governments today ask for a caste-wise survey, the debate echoes the colonial census: counting categories can shape the identities being counted.

rv.summary: Colonial rulers counted and classified caste to govern India, which made caste identities more rigid. Colonialism did not invent caste, but it changed it through the census, land settlements and the 1935 Act's schedules.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.t: Caste in the present: reform, the state and change
topics.h: In a metro train, nobody asks your caste before you sit down. But at a wedding, caste often still decides who marries whom. Modern India changed caste in public life far more than in private life.
p: Opposition to caste came from reformers and nationalists: Jyotiba Phule, B.R. Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi (in different ways) attacked untouchability and caste discrimination. Abolishing caste was part of the nationalist programme.
The independent state was committed to abolishing caste, yet it also used caste as a basis for reservations to undo historical injustice. This is a contradiction the book highlights.
Industrialisation, urbanisation and education weakened caste rules in public life: factory and office jobs, eating in restaurants and travelling in trains and buses made strict separation hard.
In the cultural and domestic sphere caste has proved resilient, especially endogamy: most marriages still take place within the caste.

ex.q: Why does the book call the state's approach to caste 'contradictory'?
st: The state aimed for a caste-free society.
But to correct past injustice it used caste to define who gets reservations.
So it both sought to abolish caste and gave caste an official role.
ex.a: It wanted to end caste but had to recognise caste to remedy caste-based disadvantage.

topics.rl: Indian Railways never had caste-wise coaches, and urban offices hire by qualification; yet marriage portals still offer filters by caste. Public change, private continuity.

rv.summary: Reformers and nationalists such as Phule, Ambedkar and Gandhi opposed caste, and the independent state aimed to abolish it while also using it for reservations. Caste has weakened in public life but stays strong in marriage and the home.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.t: Caste and politics: dominant castes and visibility
topics.h: At election time, analysts on TV talk about caste 'arithmetic' in every constituency. Democracy did not end caste; it gave caste a new job.
p: Caste became a basis for political mobilisation: caste associations formed, parties built caste-based support bases or 'vote banks', and castes acted as pressure groups.

M.N. Srinivas's 'dominant castes': castes that are numerically large, own land and hold political power in a region. Many were middle castes that gained from land reforms, e.g. Yadavs (Bihar, UP), Vokkaligas (Karnataka), Reddys and Kammas (Andhra Pradesh), Marathas (Maharashtra), Jats (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) and Patidars (Gujarat).
Sanskritisation, adopting the customs of higher castes, was one route by which castes sought upward mobility.
For urban upper castes caste has become 'invisible': having gained economic and educational capital from caste in the past, they can now claim to be 'caste-less' and rely on merit.
For SC, ST and OBC groups caste has become hyper-visible, because their caste identity is central to claims on reservations and other state protection.

ex.q: An urban professional says, 'Caste doesn't matter to me at all.' A villager from a Scheduled Caste says caste shapes everything in his life. How does the book explain both views?
st: The professional's family may have built education and wealth through past caste privilege.
Now that capital passes on without visible caste help, caste looks 'invisible' to him.
The villager depends on caste-based protections and still faces discrimination, so caste is highly visible.
Both views come from different social positions.
ex.a: Caste is invisible to those it has already benefited and hyper-visible to those who need caste-based remedies.

topics.rl: Election coverage that discusses which community dominates a district's land and politics is applying Srinivas's idea of the dominant caste.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.t: Tribe: concept and classification by permanent traits
topics.h: From the Gonds of central India, numbering in millions, to Andaman island communities of just a few hundred people, 'tribe' covers an astonishing range of communities.
p: 'Tribe' is a modern term, used by colonial and later administrators for communities seen as outside the caste-Hindu fold: no caste, no written-text religion, no state of the usual kind and no sharp class divisions.
Permanent traits used to classify tribes: region, language, physical (racial) characteristics and ecological habitat.
Region: about 85 per cent of the tribal population lives in 'middle India' (from Gujarat and Rajasthan to West Bengal and Odisha); over 11 per cent lives in the North-East.

Language: four families, Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austric and Tibeto-Burman. Austric is spoken entirely by tribal people, and over 80 per cent of Tibeto-Burman speakers are tribal. Physical-racial categories once used: Negrito, Australoid, Mongoloid, Dravidian and Aryan.

Size: tribes range from over a million (Gonds, Bhils, Santhals, Oraons, Minas, Bodos, Mundas) to very small groups such as the Andamanese islanders. Tribal people make up about 8 per cent of India's population.

ex.q: Which permanent trait is used when tribes are grouped as 'Austric' or 'Tibeto-Burman'?
st: Austric and Tibeto-Burman are names of language families.
Language is one of the permanent traits.
So the classification is by language.
ex.a: Language.

topics.rl: The Santhali language, written in Ol Chiki script, is included in the Eighth Schedule, a recognition of a large Austric-speaking tribal community.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.t: Acquired traits and the debate over 'tribe'
topics.h: Textbooks once pictured tribes as isolated forest dwellers frozen in time. But Gond kings ruled kingdoms, and tribal chiefs traded and fought alongside states for centuries. The real history is very different.
p: Acquired traits used to classify tribes: (1) mode of livelihood: fishers, food gatherers and hunters, shifting cultivators, peasants, and plantation and industrial workers; (2) extent of incorporation into Hindu society.
Debate: many scholars argue tribes were never isolated or 'primitive'. Many were 'secondary' formations, shaped through long contact with states and civilisations.
Historical evidence: Gond kingdoms of central India (such as Garha Mandla and Chanda); tribal chiefdoms; trading links; tribes serving as soldiers and allies of states.

1940s debate on policy: 'isolationists' or protectionists (associated with Verrier Elwin) wanted tribes protected from traders, moneylenders and missionaries; 'integrationists' (associated with G.S. Ghurye, who saw tribes as 'backward Hindus') wanted them integrated into the mainstream.

ex.q: A tribe once practised shifting cultivation; now many members work in a steel plant. Which classification captures this change?
st: Shifting cultivation and industrial work are modes of livelihood.
Livelihood is an acquired trait, so it can change.
The tribe moves from one livelihood category to another.
ex.a: Classification by mode of livelihood, an acquired trait.

topics.rl: The Gond kingdom of Garha Mandla in present-day Madhya Pradesh, with its forts and queens such as Rani Durgavati, shows that tribal communities built states of their own.

rv.summary: Tribes are also classified by acquired traits: mode of livelihood and extent of incorporation into Hindu society. Many scholars argue tribes were never isolated or primitive, and the 1940s saw a debate between isolationists and integrationists.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.h: The big dams and steel plants that powered India's growth were often built on tribal land. For those who lost their homes, 'national development' felt very different.
p: After independence, national development, through large dams, mines, industries and forest policies, often came at the cost of tribal communities, who lost land and forests and were displaced.
Tribal identity today is shaped by forced incorporation into the mainstream and by resistance and assertion against it.
Long movements won statehood for Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh in 2000, but problems of displacement and control over resources continue.
In the North-East, special laws (such as the Armed Forces Special Powers Act) limiting civil liberties have been linked to cycles of rebellion and repression.

Reservations have produced an educated tribal middle class that shapes tribal identity and assertion. Two key issues drive tribal movements: control over vital resources (land, forests) and ethnic-cultural identity.

ex.q: A dam floods forest villages of an adivasi community. Which two issues of tribal movements does this raise?
st: Loss of land and forest is about control over resources.
Loss of sacred sites, language and community life threatens ethnic-cultural identity.
Both issues are combined in the protest.
ex.a: Control over land and forests, and protection of cultural identity.

topics.rl: Jharkhand, formed in 2000, holds vast mineral wealth; debates over who benefits from its mines show that statehood did not end resource struggles.

rv.summary: National development through dams, mines, industries and forest policies often displaced tribal communities. Tribal identity today is shaped by forced incorporation and by resistance, with movements centred on control over resources and ethnic-cultural identity.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.h: Think of your own family: who lives with whom, whose surname you carry, who decides big things. Each answer points to a different way of classifying families.
p: Nuclear family: one couple and their unmarried children. Extended (joint) family: more than one couple, often more than two generations, living together.
It is a myth that India had only joint families: nuclear families have always existed, especially among some groups, and joint families were often an ideal of landed upper castes.

By residence: matrilocal (couple lives with the wife's parents) or patrilocal (with the husband's parents). By inheritance/succession: matrilineal (through the mother) or patrilineal (through the father). By authority: matriarchal (women dominant) or patriarchal (men dominant).
Families change accidentally (war, migration, illness) or through deliberate choices. In many urban families grandparents now move in to help with child care while both parents work.
Marriage is changing too: more love marriages and a higher age at marriage, though inter-caste marriages still face resistance.

ex.q: Priya, after marriage, lives with her husband in his parents' house; property passes from father to son; the eldest man makes major decisions. Classify this family.
st: Living with the husband's parents: patrilocal.
Property from father to son: patrilineal.
Men hold authority: patriarchal.
ex.a: Patrilocal, patrilineal and patriarchal.

topics.rl: Many IT professionals in Bengaluru or Pune live in nuclear flats but bring parents from their home towns to help raise children, a new shape of the 'joint' family.

rv.summary: Families can be nuclear or extended, and classified by residence, inheritance and authority. Nuclear families have always existed in India, and families change both accidentally and by deliberate choice.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change
topics.t: Matriliny, matriarchy and gender: the Khasi example
topics.h: Among the Khasis of Meghalaya, property passes from mother to daughter. Does that make it a society ruled by women? The answer is a lesson in reading sociological terms carefully.
p: Matrilineal societies in India include the Khasis of Meghalaya and the Nairs of Kerala.
Among the Khasis, property passes from mother to daughter, but control over it rests with the mother's brother (maternal uncle).
This creates role strain for men: they are torn between responsibilities to their natal family (sister's household) and to their wife and children.
Matriliny is not matriarchy: inheritance through women does not mean women hold power. Matriarchy remains a theoretical concept with no clear historical or ethnographic example.
In most Indian families, patriarchal norms and son preference shape decisions on inheritance, education and even survival of girls.

ex.q: Explain why a Khasi woman who inherits ancestral property may still not control it.
st: Khasi descent and inheritance run through women: matriliny.
But managing and controlling property is the job of her brother or maternal uncle.
So ownership by inheritance and authority are separated, and men keep authority.
ex.a: Matriliny gives women inheritance, but authority stays with men, so it is not matriarchy.

topics.rl: Meghalaya's matrilineal customs often surprise visitors, yet debates there about men's rights and women's role in traditional councils show that inheritance and power are different things.

rv.summary: Among the matrilineal Khasis, property passes from mother to daughter but is controlled by the mother's brother. So matriliny is not matriarchy, and Khasi men face role strain between natal and conjugal families.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: A sweeper and a bank manager may both start work at 9 a.m. One woke at 4 to fetch water and catch two buses; the other was driven to office. Is the difference just about talent?
p: Institutions such as caste, tribe, family and the market do not only organise society; they also produce inequality and exclusion.
Inequality often looks natural or deserved, as if the poor are poor because of their own failings. This leads people to 'blame the victim'.
Sociology shows that most inequality is group-based: people's chances depend on the caste, class, gender, region or community they are born into, not only on individual talent, effort or luck.
A useful activity: compare a typical day of people at different levels (a domestic worker, a clerk, a business owner) by interviewing them. The patterns reveal structured inequality.

ex.q: Two students score differently in Class 12. One had a private tutor, a quiet room and a laptop; the other worked in a shop after school. What would a sociologist say?
st: Individual effort matters, but resources differed sharply.
These resources came from family class position, not from the students themselves.
Such differences repeat across groups, so they are social, not just individual.
ex.a: The gap is shaped largely by group-based, social inequality in resources.

topics.rl: Surveys of NEET and JEE toppers often show many come from families who could afford coaching in Kota or Hyderabad, a reminder that 'merit' grows on social soil.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.t: Social inequality and Bourdieu's three capitals
topics.h: A doctor's daughter inherits not just money but books at home, polished English and contacts who can recommend her for internships. Pierre Bourdieu called these different kinds of capital.
p: Inequality is social in three senses: it is about groups, not just individuals; it is not only economic (it includes status, education and power); and it is systematic and structured.
Social inequality is the unequal distribution of socially valued resources: money, property, education, health, power and prestige.

Pierre Bourdieu identified three forms of capital: economic capital (material assets and income), cultural capital (educational qualifications and status) and social capital (networks of contacts and social associations).
These forms can be converted into one another: money can buy good education (economic → cultural), education can get a good job (cultural → economic), and contacts can open doors (social → economic).

ex.q: Classify: (a) a flat in Mumbai, (b) an IIT degree, (c) an uncle who is a senior officer and recommends you.
st: (a) Material asset: economic capital.
(b) Educational qualification: cultural capital.
(c) Network and contacts: social capital.
ex.a: (a) economic, (b) cultural, (c) social capital.

topics.rl: LinkedIn connections, alumni networks of top colleges and family business contacts are modern forms of social capital that help some people get jobs faster.

rv.summary: Social inequality is the unequal distribution of socially valued resources, and it is group-based, not only economic, and structured. Bourdieu described economic, cultural and social capital, which can be converted into one another.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: If your grandparents were landless labourers, what are the odds that you will own a business? Social stratification is the reason the answer is not '50-50'.
p: Social stratification is a society-wide system that ranks categories of people in a hierarchy. Your place in it shapes your life chances: education, health, income, even life expectancy.
Principle 1: stratification is a characteristic of society, not simply a function of individual differences. It becomes elaborate as societies produce surplus wealth to be distributed.
Principle 2: stratification persists over generations. It is closely linked to the family and inheritance of resources; ascribed status (such as caste) and endogamy keep it going.
Principle 3: stratification is supported by patterns of belief or ideology. For example, the caste system was justified by ideas of purity and pollution.

ex.q: Which principle of stratification does each show? (a) Children of rich parents inherit property; (b) caste rank was justified by ritual purity; (c) whole categories of people, not just individuals, are ranked.
st: (a) Inheritance across generations: Principle 2.
(b) Belief justifies inequality: Principle 3.
(c) A feature of society, not of individuals: Principle 1.
ex.a: (a) Principle 2; (b) Principle 3; (c) Principle 1.

topics.rl: Studies of top company boards in India find many directors from a few communities and families, showing how stratification persists across generations.

rv.summary: Social stratification is a society-wide system that ranks categories of people and shapes their life chances. It rests on three principles: it is a feature of society, it persists over generations, and it is supported by belief or ideology.

Role of family, inheritance, ascribed status and endogamy in persistence
Meaning of 'life chances'

Principle 2: it persists over generations
Principle 3: it is supported by patterns of belief or ideology (e.g. purity and pollution)
Ascribed status: status given at birth, such as caste

Don't confuse ascribed status with achieved status

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: In many old films, a character from one community is always the comic servant, another always the villain. These portrayals are not harmless fun; they shape how real people are treated.
p: Prejudice: pre-formed opinions or attitudes held by members of one group about another, based on hearsay rather than evidence, and resistant to change even when new information appears. Prejudice can be negative or positive.

Stereotypes: fixed and inflexible images of a group, applied to all its members while ignoring individual variation. Example: the colonial idea of 'martial races', which labelled some communities as naturally warlike.

Discrimination: actual behaviour or practice that disqualifies members of a group from opportunities (jobs, housing, education). It may be open or hidden, and is often justified with other reasons such as 'merit'.
Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is action. Prejudice can exist without discrimination, and discrimination can occur without open prejudice.
Activity: analyse how films or novels portray groups, and notice prejudiced or stereotyped portrayals.

ex.q: A landlord believes people of a certain community are 'unclean' (A) and refuses to rent his flat to a family from that community (B). Identify A and B.
st: A is an opinion not based on evidence and applied to a whole group: prejudice (resting on a stereotype).
B is actual behaviour denying an opportunity: discrimination.
ex.a: A: prejudice; B: discrimination.

topics.rl: Housing advertisements that say 'only vegetarians' or 'family only' have been questioned for hiding discrimination behind apparently neutral rules.

rv.summary: Prejudice is a pre-formed attitude about a group, stereotypes are fixed images applied to all its members, and discrimination is actual behaviour that denies a group opportunities. Prejudice is attitude; discrimination is action.
focus: Definitions of prejudice, stereotype and discrimination
Telling attitude (prejudice) from action (discrimination) in examples
Why discrimination is hard to prove
remember: Prejudice: pre-formed opinions based on hearsay rather than evidence, resistant to change; can be positive or negative
Stereotype: fixed, inflexible image of a group that ignores individual variation, e.g. colonial 'martial races'
Discrimination: behaviour that disqualifies a group from opportunities; may be hidden behind reasons like 'merit'
traps: Don't confuse prejudice (attitude) with discrimination (action)
Prejudice is not always hostile; it can be positive
Discrimination is not always open

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.t: Social exclusion and the limits of law
topics.h: Imagine a village where one community cannot draw water from the main well, a bank branch that ignores a woman without proper papers, and a hospital that treats a transgender patient with contempt. All are forms of social exclusion.
p: Social exclusion: the ways in which individuals or groups are cut off from full participation in the wider society, including access to services such as health, education, banking, transport and police protection.
Exclusion is involuntary and structural: it is practised regardless of the wishes of those excluded. It is not about individuals choosing to stay away.
Prolonged exclusion can lead the excluded to stop trying to participate, which can then be wrongly read as their own 'choice'.
Law alone cannot end prejudice and exclusion. Sustained campaigns to change social attitudes and practices are needed alongside legal protections.

Transgender and third-gender people have faced deep exclusion. The Supreme Court recognised the 'third gender' in 2014 (NALSA judgment), and the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in 2019.

ex.q: A Dalit family stops sending its children to a village school after years of humiliation there. Some say, 'They don't value education.' What would a sociologist say?
st: The family was excluded through humiliation: involuntary and structural.
Repeated exclusion led them to stop trying.
Calling it their 'choice' hides the exclusion behind it.
ex.a: It is the result of exclusion, not a voluntary choice.

topics.rl: Jan Dhan accounts were opened for crores of people who had never had a bank account, an attempt to reduce one form of exclusion, from the banking system.

rv.summary: Social exclusion is being cut off from full participation in society, and it is involuntary and structural. Law alone cannot end it; sustained campaigns to change attitudes are also needed.
focus: Meaning of social exclusion and why it is involuntary
Why excluded groups may stop trying, and why this is not a 'choice'
Limits of law; transgender rights milestones
remember: Social exclusion: ways individuals or groups are cut off from full participation in wider society
NALSA judgment (2014): Supreme Court recognised the 'third gender'
Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act: 2019
traps: Exclusion is not voluntary; don't blame the excluded
Don't think law alone changes society
Don't mix up the judgment year (2014) with the Act year (2019)

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: Look at any national survey of poverty by social group and the ranking barely changes: Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Castes at the bottom, upper castes at the top. Caste and class still march together.
p: Caste is a system that legitimises discrimination; it can be humiliating, exclusionary and exploitative for those at the bottom.

In the ideal model, ritual status (purity) and economic status were supposed to be separate. In practice, caste and class overlapped strongly: upper castes held land and power; lower castes were mostly poor.
Since the 19th century the link between caste and occupation has weakened, but at the macro level the caste-class correlation remains strong.

Poverty data (e.g. 2011-12) show the pattern: Scheduled Tribes have the highest proportion of poor people, followed by Scheduled Castes, then OBCs, while upper castes have the lowest poverty and the largest share of the affluent, in both rural and urban areas.

A comparison: apartheid in South Africa was a legal system of racial segregation, fought by the African National Congress and Nelson Mandela; it ended in 1994 with the first democratic elections. Race there, like caste here, tied identity to inequality.

ex.q: A table shows poverty in 2011-12: ST highest, then SC, then OBC, then upper castes lowest. What conclusion can be drawn?
st: The ranking of poverty closely follows the caste hierarchy.
This holds in both rural and urban areas.
So caste and economic status still correlate strongly.
ex.a: Caste and class remain strongly linked at the macro level.

topics.rl: Nelson Mandela, imprisoned for 27 years, became South Africa's first black president in 1994; Indians often compare the anti-apartheid struggle with the struggle against caste discrimination.

rv.summary: In the ideal caste model, ritual and economic status were separate, but in practice caste and class overlapped strongly. Poverty data still follow caste: Scheduled Tribes are poorest, then SCs, then OBCs, with upper castes least poor.
focus: Ideal model versus practice of caste and class
Reading poverty data by social group (2011-12)
Weakening caste-occupation link but strong caste-class correlation
Apartheid comparison

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: In some places, Dalits were once forbidden from even letting their shadow fall on an upper-caste person. Untouchability is the most extreme form of caste discrimination.
p: Untouchability is an extreme and especially vicious aspect of the caste system that prescribes stringent social sanctions against members of castes located at the bottom of the purity-pollution scale, who are considered polluting.
It is found across India, though its forms and intensity vary by region.

Three dimensions: exclusion (denied access to water sources, temples, ceremonies), humiliation-subordination (forced gestures of deference, such as removing footwear), and exploitation (forced, unpaid or underpaid labour).
In parts of southern India, 'distance pollution' meant that even the presence or shadow of a so-called untouchable was considered polluting.

Names: Gandhi used 'Harijan' (children of God). The groups themselves chose 'Dalit' (meaning oppressed or downtrodden), popularised by the Dalit Panthers in the 1970s. 'Dalit' asserts identity, not pity.

ex.q: Classify each practice by the dimension of untouchability: (a) not allowed to enter a temple; (b) forced to remove footwear before upper castes; (c) made to do unpaid labour at village functions.
st: (a) Denial of access: exclusion.
(b) Forced deference: humiliation-subordination.
(c) Unpaid labour: exploitation.
ex.a: (a) exclusion; (b) humiliation-subordination; (c) exploitation.

topics.rl: Dalit literature and autobiographies, now taught in universities and translated widely, use the word 'Dalit' with pride, as a symbol of resistance.

rv.summary: Untouchability is an extreme aspect of caste that imposes harsh sanctions on castes seen as polluting. It has three dimensions, exclusion, humiliation-subordination and exploitation, and the self-chosen name 'Dalit' asserts identity.
focus: The three dimensions of untouchability and classifying examples
Meaning of 'distance pollution'
'Harijan' versus 'Dalit' and the Dalit Panthers
remember: Three dimensions: exclusion, humiliation-subordination, exploitation
'Dalit' means oppressed or downtrodden; popularised by the Dalit Panthers in the 1970s
Gandhi used 'Harijan' (children of God)
traps: Sanskritisation is not a dimension of untouchability
Don't confuse humiliation (forced deference) with exclusion (denied access)
'Distance pollution' is not environmental pollution

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.t: Fighting caste discrimination: state and non-state efforts
topics.h: From a law of 1850 to the Constitution's Article 17 and the Atrocities Act of 1989, Indian law has slowly built a wall against caste discrimination. Dalit movements built the pressure that made those laws happen.
p: State initiatives: Scheduled lists of castes and tribes from 1935; reservation of seats in legislatures, government jobs and educational institutions for SCs and STs.

Key laws: Caste Disabilities Removal Act, 1850 (citizens' rights not to be curtailed due to change of religion or caste); Article 17 of the Constitution abolishing untouchability; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989; 93rd Amendment (2005) enabling OBC reservation in higher education.
Non-state initiatives: Dalit movements and leaders such as Jyotiba Phule, Periyar (E.V. Ramaswamy), Iyothee Thass and B.R. Ambedkar fought for dignity and equality.

Dalit political parties, Dalit literature in Marathi, Kannada, Tamil, Hindi and other languages, and poems such as Daya Pawar's 'The City', which shows caste surviving beneath a modern urban surface, are forms of assertion.
Activity: list the constitutional articles and laws relating to SCs, STs and untouchability.

ex.q: Arrange these legal milestones in order: Atrocities Act; Article 17 in the Constitution; Caste Disabilities Removal Act; 93rd Amendment.
st: Caste Disabilities Removal Act: 1850.
Article 17: Constitution in force from 1950.
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act: 1989.
93rd Amendment: 2005.

topics.rl: Reserved constituencies in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, and SC/ST quotas in central universities and the UPSC, are everyday reminders of state initiatives against caste inequality.

rv.summary: The state fought caste discrimination through schedules, reservations and laws such as Article 17 and the Atrocities Act. Non-state efforts include Dalit movements, leaders, parties and literature.

State versus non-state initiatives
Anti-caste leaders and Dalit literature, e.g. Daya Pawar's 'The City'

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: In 1990, the decision to implement the Mandal Commission report set off fierce debates across India's campuses. Who are the Other Backward Classes, and why did their inclusion matter so much?
p: OBCs are castes of low ritual status, above the 'untouchable' groups but below the upper castes; many are service and artisan castes. They were not subjected to untouchability, which distinguishes them from Dalits.
The Constitution uses the idea of 'socially and educationally backward classes'. OBCs exist among non-Hindu religions too, for example among Muslims and Christians.
The First Backward Classes Commission was headed by Kaka Kalelkar (1953). The Second, the B.P. Mandal Commission, reported in 1980; its recommendations were implemented in 1990.
Southern states had backward class movements and reservation policies much earlier, in the first half of the 20th century.
OBCs are internally divided: landed, dominant upper OBCs (often powerful in rural areas) versus poor lower OBCs, mainly artisans and service castes.

ex.q: How are OBCs different from Dalits?
st: Dalits faced untouchability, the most extreme form of exclusion.
OBCs had low ritual status but were not 'untouchable'.
OBCs include both landed dominant castes and poor service castes; they also exist among non-Hindus.
ex.a: OBCs are low-status but not untouchable, and are internally more varied.

topics.rl: The 27 per cent OBC reservation in central government jobs and central educational institutions traces back to the Mandal Commission and the 93rd Amendment.

rv.summary: OBCs are castes of low ritual status that were not subjected to untouchability, and they exist among non-Hindus too. The Kalelkar and Mandal Commissions dealt with them, and OBCs are internally divided between landed and poor groups.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: In the forests of central India, families who had gathered mahua and tendu leaves for generations suddenly became 'encroachers' on land declared to be state forest. Adivasi struggles begin with such stories.
p: Scheduled Tribes face poverty, powerlessness and social stigma, similar in some ways to Dalits but with different roots.
Colonial forest policy declared forests state property, turned adivasis into 'encroachers' on their own lands, and restricted shifting cultivation and gathering of forest produce.

After independence, mines, dams and industries displaced huge numbers of adivasis, often without fair compensation or rehabilitation, e.g. the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada and the Polavaram project on the Godavari.
Liberalisation after 1991 made it easier for corporations to acquire land in tribal areas.

'Adivasi' (original inhabitants) is a political term of assertion; 'diku' means outsiders (traders, moneylenders, officials). Adivasis lived in contiguous areas, unlike Dalits, which helped movements win the states of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh (2000).

ex.q: Why could adivasis win separate states while Dalits could not demand a state of their own?
st: Adivasis were concentrated in contiguous regions, such as the Chota Nagpur plateau.
Dalits are spread across villages all over India, not in one block of territory.
Territorial concentration made statehood a realistic demand for adivasis.
ex.a: Contiguous territorial concentration of adivasis made statehood possible.

topics.rl: Protests over the Sardar Sarovar dam, led by the Narmada Bachao Andolan, drew national attention to the displacement of adivasi villages in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat.

rv.summary: Adivasis face poverty, powerlessness and stigma, worsened by colonial forest policy, displacement by dams and mines, and liberalisation. Living in contiguous areas helped their movements win Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh in 2000.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: In 1905, Begum Rokeya imagined a 'Ladyland' where women ran the country and men stayed indoors. It was one of the earliest science fiction stories by an Indian woman, and a sharp critique of purdah.
p: Gender inequality is social, not natural. Evidence: matrilineal societies like the Nairs and Khasis, and women who were major farmers and traders in parts of Africa, show women's roles vary by society.

The 'women's question' arose in 19th-century middle-class reform movements. Raja Rammohun Roy (Brahmo Samaj) campaigned against sati; M.G. Ranade argued for widow remarriage using both scriptures and Western moral philosophy.

Jyotiba Phule (Satyashodhak Samaj) attacked caste and gender oppression together. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan sought reform within Islam and favoured girls' education at home; Dayanand Saraswati took a broadly similar approach to women's education.
Tarabai Shinde's 'Stree Purush Tulana' (1882) protested the double standards of a male-dominated society.
Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain's 'Sultana's Dream' (1905) is a role-reversed utopia, an early work of science fiction in English by an Indian woman.

ex.q: Match each reformer to a contribution: Rammohun Roy, Tarabai Shinde, Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain.
st: Rammohun Roy: campaigned against sati (Brahmo Samaj).
Tarabai Shinde: 'Stree Purush Tulana' (1882) against double standards.
Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain: 'Sultana's Dream' (1905), a role-reversed utopia.
ex.a: Roy: anti-sati; Shinde: Stree Purush Tulana; Rokeya: Sultana's Dream.

topics.rl: Phule and his wife Savitribai opened schools for girls in Pune; today Savitribai Phule Pune University is named after her.

rv.summary: Gender inequality is social, not natural, as women's roles vary across societies. The 'women's question' arose in 19th-century middle-class reform, with reformers and women writers challenging practices and double standards.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.t: Women's movement in the 20th century and beyond
topics.h: In 1931, decades before independence, the Indian National Congress at Karachi promised women equal rights as citizens. Turning that promise into reality took a whole movement.
p: Early 20th century: women's organisations were formed at national and local levels, and many women took part in the national movement.
The Karachi Session of the Indian National Congress (1931) adopted a resolution on Fundamental Rights and economic policy that committed to women's equality as citizens.
After a lull, the women's movement revived in the 1970s, and in the 1980s campaigns for legal reform took up issues like rape, dowry deaths and violence against women.
New challenges include the declining child sex ratio and sex-selective abortion.
Activities: study a local reformer; list jobs open and closed to women; group projects on women's reservation or domestic violence.

ex.q: List three issues the women's movement has taken up over time.
st: Early phase: education, sati, widow remarriage, participation in the national movement.
1970s-80s: rape laws, dowry deaths, violence against women.
Recent: the declining child sex ratio.
ex.a: Reform of social customs, legal reform against violence, and the sex ratio.

topics.rl: Many panchayats now have women sarpanches because of one-third reservation for women in local bodies, an outcome of long campaigns.

rv.summary: In the early 20th century women formed organisations and joined the national movement, and the 1931 Karachi resolution committed to women's equality. The movement revived in the 1970s, took up legal reform in the 1980s and now faces new challenges like the declining child sex ratio.

topics.ch: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
topics.h: In the film 'Iqbal', a boy who cannot hear or speak dreams of bowling for India. His biggest hurdle is not his body, but people who refuse to give him a chance.
p: Disability is social, not only biological: society is built in ways that exclude people with impairments (steps without ramps, no sign language, inaccessible schools and courts).

Anita Ghai notes that disabled people are often invisible in society. Common perceptions treat disability as biological, see the disabled as victims and dependents, and assume disability shapes their self-perception.

Derogatory terms and the 'bechara' (pitiable) attitude reflect cultural beliefs that impairment is fate or the result of karma, seen in myths and folklore. Newer terms such as 'differently abled' and 'visually impaired' reject insulting labels.
Poverty and disability reinforce each other: malnutrition and poor health care cause impairments, and disability reduces earning chances.
The Census 2011 counted disability in eight categories. Laws: the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995, and later the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, take a rights-based approach.

ex.q: A wheelchair user cannot reach a district court on the first floor without a ramp or lift. Is the disability in her body or in the building?
st: Her impairment is physical.
But the barrier that stops her is the design of the building.
A ramp or lift would remove the barrier.
ex.a: The disabling barrier is social: the building, not just her body.

topics.rl: Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan) aims to make public buildings, railway stations and websites accessible, treating disability as a matter of design and rights.

rv.summary: Disability is social, not only biological, because society is built in ways that exclude people with impairments. Cultural attitudes, poverty and laws all shape how disabled people are treated.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Challenges of Cultural Diversity
topics.t: Cultural diversity and why it is challenging
topics.h: When Karnataka and Tamil Nadu argue over Cauvery water, the dispute is about a river, but the passions on the street are about identity. That is why cultural diversity can be both a treasure and a challenge.
p: Cultural diversity means the presence of different types of social and cultural communities: groups defined by language, religion, sect, race or caste. It refers to differences, not inequalities.
Diversity is challenging because cultural identities are very powerful; they can arouse intense passions and mobilise large numbers of people.
Diversity often overlaps with economic and social inequalities, so one community may feel deprived compared with another.
Competition over scarce resources, such as river waters, jobs or government funds, can turn cultural differences into conflict.
India is one of the most culturally diverse nations in the world, with many languages, religions, castes, tribes and regional cultures.

ex.q: Why can a dispute over sharing river water between two states turn into an identity conflict?
st: The water is a scarce resource needed by farmers in both states.
Each state is also a linguistic-cultural community.
Competition over the resource is read as a threat to one's community.
Identity passions then intensify the economic dispute.
ex.a: Scarce resources plus powerful cultural identities can turn differences into conflict.

topics.rl: A Republic Day parade, with tableaux from every state in different languages, dress and music, celebrates the same diversity that politicians must manage every day.

rv.summary: Cultural diversity means the presence of different communities defined by language, religion, sect, race or caste; it refers to differences, not inequalities. It is challenging because identities arouse passions, overlap with inequality and can clash over scarce resources.
focus: Meaning of cultural diversity and how it differs from inequality

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Challenges of Cultural Diversity
topics.h: Nobody chooses their mother tongue, their family's religion or the region they are born in. Yet these unchosen belongings can feel like the core of who we are.
p: Community identity is ascriptive: it is based on birth and belonging, not on any form of achievement or qualification. We belong because we were born into it.
Membership is unconditional; we do not have to earn it, and it is very hard to escape. Even if we disown it, others may continue to identify us by it.
It is formed through socialisation by 'significant others' (parents, family, kin, community). The mother tongue is a key carrier of culture and identity.
Community ties give people security and meaning, so any threat to them provokes strong emotional reactions.
Identity conflicts are hard to resolve because each side sees the other as a mirror image: each feels it is the victim and the other is the aggressor.

ex.q: Ravi, born in a Tamil-speaking family, moves to Delhi and rarely speaks Tamil. Why might people still call him 'the Tamil boy'?
st: His community identity was ascribed at birth.
Membership is unconditional and hard to escape.
Others continue to identify him by it, whatever his own choices.
ex.a: Ascriptive identity persists because others keep recognising it.

topics.rl: Diaspora associations of Malayalis in the Gulf or Gujaratis in East Africa show how strongly community identity travels with people across borders.

rv.summary: Community identity is ascriptive: based on birth and belonging, unconditional and hard to escape. It is formed through socialisation by significant others, and threats to it provoke strong reactions.

topics.ch: Indian Society: The Challenges of Cultural Diversity
topics.h: The Soviet Union was one state with dozens of nationalities. The Jewish and Indian diasporas have members spread across many states. So is a nation the same as a state? Not quite.
p: A nation is a peculiar sort of community: easy to describe but hard to define. It is a large-scale 'community of communities' whose members share a desire to be one political collectivity.
Nations cannot be defined by any single common feature: there are nations without a common language, religion or ethnicity.
State (Max Weber): a body of political-legal institutions that claims control over a particular territory and a monopoly of legitimate force within it.

A nation-state is a nation that has its own state. There is no fixed relationship: one state may contain several nations (the former Soviet Union), and one nation may be spread across many states (diasporas, dual citizenship).
Modern states seek legitimacy by claiming to represent 'the people' and the nation.

ex.q: Why is it hard to define a nation by a single feature such as language?
st: Some nations have many languages (India, Switzerland).
Some nations share a language with others (many Spanish-speaking nations).
So language is neither necessary nor sufficient.
The key is a shared desire to be one political community.
ex.a: No single feature defines a nation; it is a community of communities sharing political aspirations.

topics.rl: Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) cards for the Indian diaspora show how belonging to a nation can stretch beyond the borders of the Indian state.

rv.summary: A nation is a large 'community of communities' sharing a desire to be one political collectivity; it is easy to describe but hard to define. A state claims control of a territory and a monopoly of legitimate force, and a nation-state is a nation with its own state.
