topics.ch: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society
topics.h: In Charlie Chaplin's film 'Modern Times', a worker tightens bolts so fast on an assembly line that he is swallowed by the machine. It is comedy, but also a sharp image of industrial work.
p: Karl Marx argued that under industrial capitalism workers are alienated: they do not own what they produce, have no control over the work process, and their work gives them no satisfaction.
The assembly line breaks work into small repetitive tasks; the worker becomes like a part of the machine, an image captured in Chaplin's 'Modern Times'.
Industrialisation brings some equality: people of different castes travel together in trains and work side by side in offices and factories. But it also creates new inequalities of class and income.

Scientific management (Taylorism), developed by Frederick Winslow Taylor, broke tasks into the smallest parts and timed them to raise output. Henry Ford's assembly-line mass production (Fordism) applied this to cars.

ex.q: Why might a worker who fixes the same bolt on 500 cars a day feel alienated, in Marx's sense?
st: He does not own the cars he helps produce.
He has no say over the speed or design of the work.
The repetitive task gives no creative satisfaction.
ex.a: He is separated from the product, the process and meaningful work.

topics.rl: Food-delivery riders whose routes, times and ratings are set by an app experience a modern form of the control Marx and Taylor would recognise.

rv.summary: Marx argued that industrial capitalism alienates workers from the product, the process and meaningful work, as assembly lines and Taylorism show. Industrialisation brings some equality between castes but creates new inequalities of class and income.
focus: Marx's concept of alienation
Taylorism and Fordism
Equalising effects versus new inequalities of industrialisation
remember: Alienation (Marx): workers do not own what they produce, have no control over the work process and get no satisfaction from work
Scientific management (Taylorism): F.W. Taylor broke tasks into smallest parts and timed them
Fordism: Henry Ford's assembly-line mass production
traps: Alienation does not mean migration
Don't overstate industrialisation's equalising effect; it creates class and income inequality

topics.ch: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society
topics.h: A bank clerk has a fixed salary, provident fund, paid leave and a pension. A construction worker on the same street may have none of these. Both are workers; their worlds are very different.
p: India's industrial pattern differs from the West: most workers are still in agriculture and the unorganised sector, not in large factories.

Organised (formal) sector: units employing ten or more people throughout the year, registered with the government, with regular jobs, fixed wages, benefits (provident fund, leave, pension) and union protection.
Unorganised (informal) sector: small units and self-employment, with irregular work, low wages, little job security and few legal protections. The vast majority of Indian workers are here.
In the early years after independence, the state led industrial development through the public sector, offering secure jobs to a small section of workers.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a clerk in a public sector bank; (b) a street vendor; (c) a domestic worker; (d) a worker in a government steel plant.
st: (a) Regular job with benefits: organised.
(b) Self-employed, no benefits: unorganised.
(c) No contract or benefits: unorganised.
(d) Public sector job with benefits: organised.
ex.a: (a) and (d) organised; (b) and (c) unorganised.

topics.rl: e-Shram, the national database of unorganised workers, aims to bring crores of informal workers into the reach of social security schemes.

rv.summary: Unlike the West, most Indian workers are in agriculture and the unorganised sector, not large factories. Organised sector jobs are regular, with benefits and union protection, while unorganised work is irregular, low-paid and insecure.
focus: Organised versus unorganised sector features
Classifying jobs into sectors
Role of the public sector after independence
remember: Organised sector: units employing ten or more people throughout the year, registered, with regular jobs and benefits
The vast majority of Indian workers are in the unorganised sector
traps: Don't assume Western patterns; most Indian workers are outside large factories
A street vendor or domestic worker is unorganised, not organised

topics.ch: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society
topics.h: After 1991, India opened its doors to foreign companies and sold shares in public sector firms. Call centres boomed, but many factory jobs turned into short-term contracts.
p: Liberalisation and globalisation from 1991 included disinvestment (selling government shares in public sector units), privatisation, and the entry of multinational companies.
Firms increasingly outsourced work to smaller units or contractors, and hired contract workers instead of permanent staff.
This reduced job security: permanent jobs shrank in many sectors, and informal and contract work grew, even inside large factories.
Some new opportunities emerged, e.g. in IT and services, but mainly for the educated and skilled.

ex.q: How did liberalisation affect a worker in a public sector factory?
st: Disinvestment or privatisation changed ownership.
New owners cut permanent staff and hired contract workers.
The worker faced less job security, or lost a permanent job.
ex.a: Job security fell as contract work replaced permanent employment.

topics.rl: Many large factories today have more contract workers than permanent employees on the same assembly line.

rv.summary: Liberalisation from 1991 brought disinvestment, privatisation, multinationals and outsourcing. Job security fell as contract and informal work grew, while new IT and service jobs went mainly to the educated and skilled.
focus: Meaning of disinvestment, outsourcing and informalisation
Effects of liberalisation on job security
Who gained from new IT and service jobs
remember: Liberalisation began in 1991
Disinvestment: government selling its shares in public sector units
Outsourcing: giving work to outside firms or contractors
traps: Don't reverse disinvestment; it is selling, not buying, government shares
Liberalisation reduced job security, not increased it
Gains from IT jobs were not uniform

topics.ch: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society
topics.h: Ask a construction worker in Mumbai how he got his job and he will probably name a mistri from his own village, not a job portal.
p: Most Indians are self-employed (e.g. farmers, shopkeepers, vendors) or do casual work.
Only a few find jobs through formal recruitment such as employment exchanges, advertisements and exams.
Contractors, jobbers and mistris recruit many workers, often from their own village or caste, and may control wages and conditions.
Social networks of kin, caste and region are crucial for getting jobs. In mills, 'badli' workers substituted for permanent workers on leave, hoping for permanent jobs later.

ex.q: Why do workers in the unorganised sector rely so much on contractors and kin networks?
st: Formal recruitment covers only a small share of jobs.
Contractors and kin provide information and introductions.
Trust and shared village or caste ties make networks important.
ex.a: Informal networks replace formal recruitment for most workers.

topics.rl: Many delivery and security jobs in cities still spread by word of mouth among people from the same district, even when apps are involved.

rv.summary: Most Indians are self-employed or do casual work, and only a few find jobs through formal recruitment. Contractors, jobbers, mistris and social networks of kin, caste and region are crucial in finding work.
focus: Self-employment and casual work as the main forms
Role of contractors, jobbers and mistris
Social networks and 'badli' workers
remember: 'Badli' worker: substitutes for a permanent worker on leave, hoping for a permanent job later
Contractors, jobbers and mistris: middlemen who recruit workers, often from their own village or caste
traps: Don't overstate formal recruitment; it reaches only a small share
Contractors control wages because workers depend on them for jobs

topics.ch: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society
topics.h: In a modern car plant, a finished car can roll off the line every minute or less. Behind that speed lies a carefully designed system to control every second of a worker's time.
p: Managers aim to control workers and get more output from them.
Two main methods: lengthening the working day, or increasing the speed and intensity of work within the same hours. Machines and assembly lines set the pace.
Example of a car factory: tight shifts, very short breaks, constant pressure to keep up with the line, and high stress; workers may fall sick or burn out.
White-collar and IT work also involve long hours and tight deadlines. 'Flexible time' often means working late into the night to meet clients' schedules in other time zones.

ex.q: A car factory worker gets two short tea breaks and must match the line's speed. Which method of control is at work?
st: The working day is not necessarily longer.
But work intensity is raised by the line's speed.
So control works by increasing the speed of work.
ex.a: Control through increasing the speed and intensity of work.

topics.rl: IT employees in Bengaluru often work on US time for project calls, an example of 'flexible' hours that stretch the working day.

rv.summary: Managers control workers to raise output, either by lengthening the working day or by increasing the speed and intensity of work. Factory work and even white-collar IT work can mean long hours, tight deadlines and high stress.

Who sets the pace on an assembly line
Stress in white-collar and IT work; meaning of 'flexible time'

traps: Compulsory overtime is lengthening the day, not intensifying work

topics.ch: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society
topics.h: A woman rolls a thousand bidis a day at home, paid a few rupees per hundred. A miner digs coal without proper safety gear. Both are workers whom labour laws often fail to reach.
p: Mines, quarries and many factories have hazardous conditions. Laws such as the Mines Act, 1952 set rules on hours, safety and welfare, but enforcement is often poor, especially in small and illegal units.
Contract workers in mines and construction often lack safety equipment, regular wages and benefits.
Accidents, occupational diseases (e.g. lung diseases from dust) and lack of compensation are common problems.
Home-based work: production done at home for traders or firms, such as bidi rolling, agarbatti making, papad rolling, zari and embroidery.
Home-based workers are mostly women and children, paid on piece rates (per unit produced), with no job security or benefits.

ex.q: Why are home-based workers especially vulnerable?
st: They work alone at home, so they are hard to organise.
They are paid per piece, often very low rates.
Labour laws rarely cover them, so they lack security and benefits.
ex.a: Isolation, piece rates and lack of legal protection.

topics.rl: SEWA (Self-Employed Women's Association) in Ahmedabad has organised lakhs of home-based and informal women workers to bargain for better rates.

rv.summary: Mines, quarries and many factories are hazardous, and laws like the Mines Act, 1952 are poorly enforced. Home-based work, done mostly by women and children on piece rates, offers no security or benefits.

Vulnerability of contract workers in mines and construction
Home-based work: examples, workers and payment

topics.ch: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society
topics.h: In January 1982, around two and a half lakh textile workers in Bombay went on strike. It lasted about two years, and many mills never reopened.
p: A strike is when workers stop work collectively to press their demands. A lockout is when management shuts the workplace to pressure workers.
Trade unions grew in India from the early 20th century and helped win better wages, hours and safety for organised workers.

The Bombay textile strike of 1982, led by trade union leader Datta Samant, involved around 2.5 lakh mill workers and lasted about two years. It ended in defeat: many mills closed and workers lost their jobs, often moving to informal work or returning to villages.
With informalisation and liberalisation, unions have weakened: contract and home-based workers are harder to organise, and many new firms resist unions.

ex.q: Why did the Bombay textile strike end in loss for many workers?
st: The strike lasted about two years, exhausting workers' savings.
Mill owners did not concede; many mills closed or shifted production.
Workers lost jobs and many moved into informal work.
ex.a: The prolonged strike led to mill closures and job losses.

topics.rl: Many of central Mumbai's former mill compounds have been redeveloped as malls and offices, a physical reminder of the decline of the textile industry after 1982.

rv.summary: A strike is workers stopping work collectively; a lockout is management shutting the workplace. Unions won gains for organised workers, but the 1982 Bombay textile strike ended in mill closures, and unions have weakened with informalisation.

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: The eight-hour working day, the right to vote for women and laws against untouchability did not fall from the sky. Each was won by a social movement.
p: Social movements have shaped modern rights and institutions, e.g. labour laws, women's rights and anti-discrimination laws.
A social movement is a collective attempt to bring about change, or to resist it.
Features: sustained collective action over a period of time, not a one-off protest or riot.
Participants share objectives and an ideology: a common understanding of what is wrong and what should change.
There is some organisation: leadership and a structure for making decisions and planning action.

ex.q: A crowd blocks a road for one afternoon after an accident and then disperses. Is this a social movement?
st: It is collective, but not sustained over time.
There is no shared long-term ideology or organisation.
So it is a protest, not a social movement.
ex.a: No: it lacks sustained action, shared ideology and organisation.

topics.rl: The campaign that produced the RTI Act lasted over a decade, had leaders and organisations, and a clear goal: a textbook social movement.

rv.summary: A social movement is a collective attempt to bring about change or to resist it. It needs sustained collective action, shared objectives and ideology, and some organisation.
focus: Definition of a social movement
The three features: sustained action, shared ideology, organisation
Telling a movement apart from a one-off protest or riot

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: When Rammohun Roy campaigned against sati, the Dharma Sabha campaigned to keep it. Every movement can spark a counter-movement.
p: Counter-movements arise to defend the status quo against a social movement, e.g. the Dharma Sabha, which petitioned the British against the law banning sati.
Movements use many methods of protest: marches, dharnas, hunger strikes, petitions, public meetings, and cultural forms like songs, poetry and street plays.
Gandhi's use of satyagraha, non-violent resistance, made methods like fasting and civil disobedience famous.
Early sociologists saw social movements as threats to social order. Later sociologists saw them as important sources of social change and of new ideas.

ex.q: Identify the movement and counter-movement: reformers demand an end to sati; orthodox groups petition to keep it.
st: Reformers seeking change: the social movement.
Orthodox groups defending the existing practice: the counter-movement (e.g. the Dharma Sabha).
ex.a: Anti-sati campaign versus the Dharma Sabha counter-movement.

topics.rl: Street plays (nukkad nataks) by college groups on topics like dowry or the environment are a modern cultural method of protest.

rv.summary: Counter-movements arise to defend the status quo, like the Dharma Sabha against the sati ban. Movements use many methods of protest, and while early sociologists saw them as threats to order, later ones saw them as sources of change.
focus: Meaning of counter-movement and the Dharma Sabha example
Methods of protest, including cultural forms and satyagraha
Early versus later sociological views of movements

traps: Don't confuse the early view (threat to order) with the later view (source of change)

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: Millions of people feel cheated by the system, yet most never join a movement. Why do some grievances become movements while others stay silent?
p: Theory of relative deprivation: social conflict arises when a group feels it is worse off than others; this sense of deprivation can drive collective protest.
Limits: feelings of deprivation are not enough to cause a movement; many deprived groups never mobilise. The theory also does not explain how movements organise.
Mancur Olson, 'The Logic of Collective Action' (1965): a movement is a sum of rational individuals pursuing self-interest; a person joins only if the gains outweigh the costs.
Resource mobilisation theory (John McCarthy and Mayer Zald): a movement's success depends on its ability to mobilise resources: leadership, organisational capacity, communication and networks.
Critique of resource mobilisation: movements can emerge and succeed even with limited resources, creating resources as they grow.

ex.q: Compare how relative deprivation and resource mobilisation theories would explain a farmers' movement.
st: Relative deprivation: farmers feel worse off than urban groups, which fuels anger.
Resource mobilisation: the movement grows because it has leaders, organisations, money and networks.
The first explains motivation; the second explains capacity to act.
ex.a: Deprivation explains grievances; resource mobilisation explains organisation and success.

topics.rl: Movements that use social media to raise funds, coordinate volunteers and spread messages are applying the logic of resource mobilisation.

rv.summary: Relative deprivation theory says movements arise when groups feel worse off than others, but deprivation alone is not enough. Olson saw movements as rational individuals weighing gains and costs, and resource mobilisation theory stresses the ability to mobilise resources.

Movements can succeed with limited resources, creating resources as they grow

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: One movement asks people to change their inner selves; another asks for a new law; a third aims to overthrow the whole system. Sociologists classify movements by how deep a change they seek.
p: Redemptive movements aim to change the inner consciousness and actions of individuals. Example: the Ezhava movement in Kerala led by Narayana Guru, which changed religious practices and self-perception.

Reformist movements aim to change existing social and political arrangements through gradual, step-by-step means. Examples: the campaign for linguistic reorganisation of states, and the Right to Information campaign.
Revolutionary movements aim to radically transform social relations, often by seizing state power. Examples: the Bolshevik revolution in Russia and the Naxalite movement in India.
Many movements combine elements of more than one type and can change over time.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a movement asking followers to give up liquor and adopt new forms of worship; (b) a campaign for a new law; (c) a movement aiming to overthrow the state.
st: (a) Changing individuals' inner lives: redemptive.
(b) Gradual change in arrangements: reformist.
(c) Radical transformation through state power: revolutionary.
ex.a: (a) redemptive; (b) reformist; (c) revolutionary.

topics.rl: Narayana Guru's consecration of temples open to all in Kerala, a key part of the Ezhava movement, inspired self-respect among lower castes.

rv.summary: Redemptive movements change individuals' inner consciousness, reformist movements seek gradual change in existing arrangements, and revolutionary movements aim to radically transform society, often by seizing state power. Many movements combine types.
focus: Defining and classifying the three types
Standard examples of each type
Movements combining types and changing over time
remember: Redemptive: e.g. Narayana Guru's Ezhava movement in Kerala
Reformist: e.g. linguistic reorganisation of states, RTI campaign
Revolutionary: e.g. Bolshevik revolution, Naxalite movement
traps: Don't treat the types as rigid; movements can combine them
The RTI campaign is reformist, not revolutionary
Redemptive is about individuals' consciousness, not state power

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: In the 1930s, most movements were about class and freedom from colonial rule. By the 1970s, people were also marching for forests, women's rights and human rights. Sociologists called these 'new' social movements.
p: 'Old' social movements were organised mainly around class (workers, peasants) and anti-colonial goals, and worked through political parties. Their focus was redistribution of power and resources.

'New' social movements, prominent from the 1970s, focus on quality of life, environment, identity and human rights, e.g. women's, environmental and anti-nuclear movements. They often work outside political parties.
New movements are often international in reach and are less about seizing state power than about changing values and policies.

In India, old and new movements overlap: issues of identity (caste, tribe, gender) are often combined with issues of resources (land, forests, wages). Chipko, for example, was both ecological and economic.

ex.q: Why is it hard to separate 'old' and 'new' movements in India?
st: Indian movements about environment or identity also involve livelihoods and resources.
E.g. tribal movements combine identity with land and forest rights.
So class issues and new issues are intertwined.
ex.a: Identity and resource issues are usually combined in Indian movements.

topics.rl: Global campaigns on climate change that connect students across countries are typical 'new' social movements.

rv.summary: Old social movements were organised around class and anti-colonial goals and worked through political parties. New social movements, prominent from the 1970s, focus on quality of life, environment, identity and rights, but in India the two often overlap.
focus: Features of old versus new social movements
Examples of new social movements
Why old and new overlap in India, e.g. Chipko and tribal movements
remember: Old movements: class and anti-colonial goals, through political parties, redistribution of power and resources
New movements (from the 1970s): quality of life, environment, identity, human rights; often outside parties and international
traps: Don't attribute party-based organisation to new movements
In India, don't treat old and new movements as separate; identity and resource issues combine

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: In the early 1970s, when contractors arrived to cut trees in the Himalayan villages of present-day Uttarakhand, village women hugged the trees and refused to let go. 'Chipko' means 'to hug' or 'to stick'.
p: Development has costs for nature and people: deforestation, large dams, mining and displacement of communities.
The Chipko movement in the Himalayan region (now Uttarakhand) began in the early 1970s; villagers, especially women, hugged trees to stop them being cut by contractors.

Chipko combined ecological concerns (protecting forests), economic concerns (forests gave fuel, fodder and livelihoods for subsistence) and political concerns (resentment against a distant state and outside contractors, and demand for local control).
Ecological movements question the dominant model of development that treats nature only as a resource for industry and cities.

ex.q: Explain why Chipko is called both an ecological and an economic movement.
st: Ecological: it protected forests from felling.
Economic: villagers depended on forests for fuel, fodder and water for subsistence.
Losing forests threatened their livelihood, so saving trees meant saving livelihoods.
ex.a: Forests were both an ecosystem and the villagers' economic base.

topics.rl: Chipko inspired the Appiko movement in Karnataka, where villagers hugged trees in the Western Ghats in the 1980s.

rv.summary: The Chipko movement began in the Himalayan region in the early 1970s, with villagers, especially women, hugging trees to stop felling. It was at once ecological, economic and political, and questioned the dominant model of development.
focus: Where, when and how Chipko began
Its ecological, economic and political dimensions
What ecological movements question
remember: Chipko: Himalayan region (now Uttarakhand), early 1970s; villagers, especially women, hugged trees
Ecological movements question the dominant model of development
traps: Don't see only ecology; Chipko was also about subsistence and local control
Village women were at the forefront, not opponents of the movement

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.t: Peasant movements and new farmers' movements
topics.h: In 1917 Gandhi went to Champaran in Bihar, where peasants were forced to grow indigo. In 1928, peasants of Bardoli in Gujarat refused to pay increased revenue. Peasant struggles shaped India's freedom movement.
p: Colonial peasant movements: the Bengal indigo revolt (1859-62), the Deccan riots (1875), Champaran satyagraha (1917) and Bardoli satyagraha (1928).
The All India Kisan Sabha was formed in 1936 to organise peasants on issues like land revenue, rents and debt.

Post-war struggles: Tebhaga (Bengal, 1946-47), where sharecroppers demanded two-thirds of the crop; Telangana (1946-51) against feudal landlords in Hyderabad state; and Naxalbari (West Bengal, 1967), an armed peasant uprising.

New farmers' movements from the 1970s, in Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and elsewhere, were led by market-oriented farmers. Their issues were prices, cost of inputs and subsidies; they were regionally organised and largely non-party, using methods like road and rail blockades.

ex.q: How did new farmers' movements differ from earlier peasant movements?
st: Earlier movements: mainly tenants and poor peasants against landlords and the colonial state over rent and revenue.
New farmers' movements: market-oriented farmers against the state over prices, inputs and subsidies.
New movements were regional and non-party.
ex.a: They shifted from land and rent to prices and inputs, and from party links to non-party organisation.

topics.rl: Farmers' groups blocking highways for better minimum support prices continue the methods of the new farmers' movements.

rv.summary: Colonial India saw peasant movements from the indigo revolt to Bardoli, and the All India Kisan Sabha formed in 1936. Post-war struggles included Tebhaga, Telangana and Naxalbari, while new farmers' movements from the 1970s focused on prices and inputs.
focus: Dates and issues of colonial peasant movements
Tebhaga, Telangana and Naxalbari
How new farmers' movements differ from earlier peasant movements
remember: Indigo revolt 1859-62; Deccan riots 1875; Champaran 1917; Bardoli 1928
All India Kisan Sabha: 1936
Tebhaga (Bengal, 1946-47): two-thirds of the crop; Telangana 1946-51; Naxalbari (West Bengal) 1967

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: In 1974, about 17 lakh railway workers went on strike, bringing India's lifeline to a halt. The workers' movement had come a long way since the first mill strikes of the 19th century.
p: Early workers' protests began with strikes in textile mills and other factories in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
The Madras Labour Union, one of India's first trade unions, was formed in 1918. The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was formed in 1920.
After independence, unions split along party lines, with different political parties having their own trade union wings.
The railway strike of 1974 was one of the largest strikes in India's history.
With the growth of the informal sector and contract work, trade unions have weakened, since such workers are hard to organise.

ex.q: Why did trade unions split after independence?
st: Different political parties formed their own union federations.
Unions became linked to party ideologies.
Workers were divided along party lines.
ex.a: Splits followed party lines as parties built union wings.

topics.rl: AITUC, formed in 1920, celebrated its centenary in 2020, making it one of the oldest workers' organisations in India.

rv.summary: The workers' movement began with strikes in textile mills, and early unions included the Madras Labour Union (1918) and AITUC (1920). After independence unions split along party lines, and informal and contract work has weakened them.

Party-wise splits after independence
The 1974 railway strike
Why unions have weakened

Unions did not stay united; they split along party lines

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: For Dalit movements, the struggle has always been about more than wages. It is about being treated as an equal human being: entering temples, drawing water from common wells and living with dignity.
p: The Dalit movement is a struggle for recognition as fellow human beings: for dignity, equality and self-respect, not just economic gains.
Examples: the Satnami movement (Chhattisgarh), the Adi-Dharma movement (Punjab), the Mahar movement (Maharashtra), and the political and social movement led by B.R. Ambedkar.
The Dalit Panthers (1970s) and a rich Dalit literature in Marathi and other languages became powerful forms of assertion.
Backward class and caste movements, especially non-Brahmin movements in the south (e.g. in Tamil Nadu), challenged Brahmin dominance in education, jobs and politics.
Some upper-caste groups have responded with a sense of 'reverse discrimination' and anti-reservation protests, e.g. after the Mandal recommendations were implemented in 1990.

ex.q: Why is the Dalit movement described as a struggle for recognition, not just economic gain?
st: Untouchability denied Dalits basic human dignity.
Their demands included temple entry, equal access to water and an end to humiliation.
So the struggle was about self-respect and equality as human beings.
ex.a: Because its core demand is dignity and equal humanity.

topics.rl: Ambedkar's Mahad satyagraha of 1927, asserting Dalits' right to draw water from a public tank, is a landmark of the struggle for dignity.

rv.summary: The Dalit movement is a struggle for recognition as fellow human beings: dignity, equality and self-respect. Backward caste and non-Brahmin movements challenged Brahmin dominance, while some upper-caste groups spoke of 'reverse discrimination'.

Matching Dalit movements to regions
Non-Brahmin movements and anti-reservation reactions after 1990

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: In 1899-1900, Birsa Munda led an uprising, the Ulgulan, against British officials, landlords and moneylenders in the Chota Nagpur region. A century later, in 2000, the state of Jharkhand was born.
p: Tribal movements have been concentrated in the central Indian 'tribal belt' (e.g. the Chota Nagpur and Santhal Parganas regions of Jharkhand) and in the North-East.
The Jharkhand movement: a long struggle against dikus (outsiders: moneylenders, traders, migrant settlers) and against land loss; it led to the creation of Jharkhand state in 2000.
Birsa Munda, who led a revolt against the British and dikus, became an enduring symbol of tribal resistance.
Key issues: land alienation, forest rights, displacement by mining and dams, and protection of cultural identity.
North-East movements focus on ethnic identity, autonomy and land rights.

ex.q: Why did the Jharkhand movement target 'dikus'?
st: Dikus were outsiders: moneylenders, traders and settlers.
They took tribal land through debt and fraud.
Opposing them meant defending land and identity.
ex.a: Dikus were seen as responsible for land loss and exploitation.

topics.rl: 15 November, Birsa Munda's birth anniversary, is also Jharkhand's foundation day and has been observed as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas since 2021.

rv.summary: Tribal movements are concentrated in the central tribal belt and the North-East. The Jharkhand movement fought dikus and land loss and led to Jharkhand state in 2000, and Birsa Munda remains a symbol of tribal resistance.

topics.ch: Social Change: Social Movements
topics.h: In 1974, a government committee's report, 'Towards Equality', revealed how far Indian women still lagged behind men despite constitutional promises. It sparked a new wave of the women's movement.
p: Early 20th-century women's organisations: the Women's India Association (1917), the All India Women's Conference (1926) and the National Council of Women in India (1925).
Women participated actively in the freedom struggle, and also in peasant and tribal movements such as Tebhaga and Telangana.

The movement revived in the 1970s after the 'Towards Equality' report (1974) of the Committee on the Status of Women in India. New autonomous women's groups, independent of political parties, emerged.
Campaigns against custodial rape (the Mathura case), dowry deaths and violence against women led to legal reforms in the 1980s.
The focus shifted from 'welfare' to 'rights' and 'empowerment', and the movement increasingly recognised the diverse issues of Dalit, tribal and working-class women.

ex.q: Trace the shift in focus of the women's movement.
st: Early phase: women's organisations, education and participation in the national movement.
1970s onward: autonomous groups, campaigns on violence, custodial rape and dowry.
Later: from welfare to rights and empowerment, recognising diverse women's issues.
ex.a: From welfare and reform to rights, empowerment and diversity.

topics.rl: Campaigns after the Mathura case led to changes in rape law in 1983, a landmark showing how the movement shaped legislation.

rv.summary: Early 20th-century women's organisations emerged and women joined the freedom struggle and peasant movements. After the 1974 'Towards Equality' report, autonomous groups revived the movement, campaigned against violence and shifted focus from welfare to rights and empowerment.

qa.q: Students' existing knowledge of Indian society mainly comes from:
qa.a: Socialisation in family, school and community
qa.e: We absorb most of what we 'know' about society from everyday socialisation.

qa.q: Why does sociology ask students to 'unlearn'?
qa.a: Taken-for-granted ideas can block a fresh, critical view
qa.e: Unlearning means questioning what we take for granted, not throwing away all experience.

qa.q: Self-reflexivity is best described as:
qa.a: Seeing oneself as others might and questioning one's position
qa.e: Self-reflexivity turns the sociological gaze back on ourselves.

qa.q: The 'social map' idea in sociology refers to:
qa.a: Locating a person within the wider society and its history
qa.e: The map is metaphorical: it shows our place in society.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A student from a privileged background may not notice the advantages she enjoys.
Reason (R): Common-sense knowledge tends to reflect one's own social position.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Our 'common sense' is shaped by where we stand, so privilege can stay invisible to the privileged.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a theme of the later chapters of the book Indian Society?
qa.a: Planetary motion and gravitation
qa.e: The book covers demography, institutions, inequality and diversity, plus project work.

qa.q: A city teenager says, 'Everyone has a smartphone these days.' A self-reflexive response would be to:
qa.a: Ask which groups she means, and who is left out
qa.e: Self-reflexivity asks whose experience a claim describes.

qa.q: Why is self-reflexivity especially important when studying one's own society?
qa.a: Familiarity makes our own biases harder to see
qa.e: We are inside our own society, so we must work harder to see it from outside.

qa.q: In what context did modern Indian society and Indian self-awareness take shape?
qa.a: Colonial rule
qa.e: The chapter places the making of modern Indian society within colonialism.

qa.q: Colonial unification of India was:
qa.a: Real, but achieved through exploitation
qa.e: Administrative and economic unification happened, but at the cost of exploitation.

qa.q: Which was a colonial administrative or economic change?
qa.a: New land revenue settlements
qa.e: Land revenue settlements were introduced by the colonial state.

qa.q: The 'paradox' of colonialism refers to the fact that:
qa.a: It created forces, like educated nationalists, that opposed it
qa.e: Colonial education and unification helped produce the nationalism that ended colonial rule.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Railways helped the growth of Indian nationalism.
Reason (R): The British built railways mainly to promote Indian self-rule.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Railways did help nationalism by connecting people, but they were built for colonial economic and military purposes.

qa.q: Which group best illustrates how colonialism produced its own opponents?
qa.a: Western-educated Indians who led nationalist bodies
qa.e: Indians trained in colonial schools used liberal ideas against the Raj.

qa.q: A uniform legal and court system under colonial rule is an example of:
qa.a: Administrative unification
qa.e: A common legal framework helped bind regions into one administrative unit.

qa.q: Why does the book insist on studying colonialism to understand Indian society today?
qa.a: Many present institutions and identities took shape under it
qa.e: Railways, courts, education and even identities show colonial roots.

qa.q: Indian nationalism developed mainly through:
qa.a: The shared struggle against colonial rule
qa.e: Common anti-colonial experience helped people imagine India as one nation.

qa.q: Which of these is a 'class' that emerged and organised in colonial India?
qa.a: Industrial workers
qa.e: Workers are a class based on economic position; the others are community identities.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of community identity organising in colonial times?
qa.a: A caste association submitting petitions
qa.e: Caste associations were a new, modern way for communities to organise.

qa.q: Reform and revival movements in colonial India:
qa.a: Reshaped how communities understood themselves
qa.e: Such movements reinterpreted traditions and community identities.

qa.q: The new middle class of colonial India was largely made up of:
qa.a: Western-educated lawyers, teachers and clerks
qa.e: Colonial education created a professional middle class.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Nationalism and community identities in colonial India were always in perfect harmony.
Reason (R): Communities and classes organised around their own interests too.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Since groups also pursued their own interests, nationalism sometimes faced tension with community and class claims.

qa.q: Peasants protesting against high land revenue in colonial India were organising on the basis of:
qa.a: Class interest
qa.e: Their shared economic position made it a class-based mobilisation.

qa.q: Which means of organising became important for both communities and classes under colonialism?
qa.a: Print media, public meetings and petitions
qa.e: Modern communication allowed new forms of collective organisation.

qa.q: Demography is the study of a population's:
qa.a: Size, composition, distribution and change
qa.e: Demography covers all four aspects of population.

qa.q: Which is an example of social demography?
qa.a: Studying why some families prefer sons
qa.e: Social demography asks about social causes and consequences.

qa.q: Why did demography develop along with the modern nation-state?
qa.a: States needed data to plan for and govern their people
qa.e: Counting the population helped modern states plan and administer.

qa.q: Since which year has India held a regular census every ten years?
qa.e: First attempts were made in 1867-72; the regular decennial census began in 1881.

qa.q: The first census of independent India was held in:
qa.e: The decennial series continued after independence, with 1951 as the first.

qa.q: Durkheim's study of suicide rates shows that:
qa.a: Rates can reveal social patterns beyond individual motives
qa.e: Stable differences in rates between groups point to social causes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The census is a key source for demography.
Reason (R): It counts the whole population and records age, sex, literacy and more.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Because it covers everyone and many attributes, the census is the backbone of population data.

qa.q: A table showing that a state's population rose from 5 crore to 6 crore is most useful for:
qa.a: Formal demography
qa.e: Counting and measuring change is the work of formal demography.

qa.q: According to Malthus, population increases in a:
qa.a: Geometric progression
qa.e: Malthus: population 2, 4, 8, 16; food 1, 2, 3, 4.

qa.q: Which is a 'positive check' in Malthus's theory?
qa.a: Famine
qa.e: Positive checks raise deaths: famines, diseases, wars.

qa.q: Which is a 'preventive check' in Malthus's theory?
qa.a: Late marriage
qa.e: Preventive checks lower births by human choice.

qa.q: If population doubles each generation from 3 crore, what will it be after 3 generations of geometric growth (in crore)?
qa.e: 3 → 6 → 12 → 24: doubling three times multiplies by 8.

qa.q: Which historical evidence went against Malthus?
qa.a: European population and living standards rose together
qa.e: Rising food output and incomes alongside growing population contradicted him.

qa.q: Liberal and Marxist critics argued that poverty and starvation are caused mainly by:
qa.a: Unequal distribution of economic resources
qa.e: They shifted the focus from numbers to inequality.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Malthus believed prosperity required controlling population growth.
Reason (R): He thought food supply could never keep up with unchecked population growth.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Because food lagged behind population, he saw population control as the key to prosperity.

qa.q: What was one key factor Malthus underestimated?
qa.a: The power of technology to raise food output
qa.e: Agricultural technology raised food supply far beyond arithmetic growth.

qa.q: The theory of demographic transition links population growth to:
qa.a: The level of economic development
qa.e: Each stage corresponds to a level of development.

qa.q: Which stage of demographic transition shows a 'population explosion'?
qa.a: The transitional stage, with falling deaths and high births
qa.e: The gap between falling death rates and high birth rates causes rapid growth.

qa.q: In the first stage of demographic transition, population grows slowly because:
qa.a: Both birth and death rates are high
qa.e: High births are cancelled out by high deaths.

qa.q: Why do death rates usually fall faster than birth rates?
qa.a: Medicine cuts deaths fast; fertility norms change slowly
qa.e: Technology acts quickly on mortality; fertility is rooted in social attitudes.

qa.q: A country has a birth rate of 36 and a death rate of 12 per 1000. What is its rate of natural increase per 1000?
qa.e: Natural increase = birth rate − death rate = 36 − 12 = 24 per 1000.

qa.q: A developed country with low birth and low death rates is in which stage?
qa.a: Third stage
qa.e: Low birth and death rates mark the final stage.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Population explosion happens in the transitional stage.
Reason (R): In this stage, the birth rate falls faster than the death rate.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: The explosion happens because the death rate falls faster while the birth rate stays high; R reverses this.

qa.q: Both Stage 1 and Stage 3 show slow growth. What is the key difference?
qa.a: Stage 1 has high birth and death rates; Stage 3 has low ones
qa.e: Slow growth can come from high-high or low-low rates.

qa.q: A district of 5,00,000 people has 11,000 live births in a year. What is its birth rate per 1000?
A state has a birth rate of 19 and a death rate of 7 per 1000. What is its rate of natural increase in per cent?
qa.e: Natural increase = 19 − 7 = 12 per 1000 = 1.2 per cent.

qa.q: The fertility rate is calculated per 1000 of:
qa.a: Women aged 15 to 49 years
qa.e: Fertility rate uses women of child-bearing age as the base.

qa.q: Among 2,500 women aged 15-49 in a village, 200 live births occur in a year. What is the fertility rate per 1000 women?
qa.e: Fertility rate = 200 / 2500 × 1000 = 80.

qa.q: Replacement-level total fertility rate is about:
qa.e: About 2.1 children per woman replace both parents, allowing for some child deaths.

qa.q: Total fertility rate refers to:
qa.a: Average number of children a woman would bear
qa.e: TFR is a lifetime average per woman, based on current fertility rates.

qa.q: When the rate of natural increase is close to zero, the population is said to have reached:
qa.a: Replacement level
qa.e: Births just balance deaths, so the population replaces itself.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Replacement TFR is slightly above 2.
Reason (R): Some children die before they reach reproductive age.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The extra 0.1 compensates for child mortality.

qa.q: Infant mortality rate is the number of deaths of children under one year of age per:
qa.a: 1000 live births
qa.e: IMR uses live births as the base, per 1000.

qa.q: Maternal mortality rate is measured per:
qa.a: 1,00,000 live births
qa.e: Because maternal deaths are rarer, the base is 1,00,000 live births.

qa.q: In a district with 40,000 live births, 1,000 infants died before their first birthday. What is the IMR?
In a state with 2,50,000 live births, 300 women died in childbirth. What is the MMR?
A town has 47,000 females and 50,000 males. What is its sex ratio?
qa.e: Sex ratio = 47000 / 50000 × 1000 = 940 females per 1000 males.

qa.q: Life expectancy refers to:
qa.a: Estimated average years a person is expected to live
qa.e: It is an estimate based on age-specific death rates.

qa.q: A sex ratio of 1084 in a district means:
qa.a: There are more females than males
qa.e: Above 1000 means more than 1000 females per 1000 males.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A low IMR is a sign of good health care and development.
Reason (R): Infant survival depends on nutrition, sanitation and medical care.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Since infant survival depends on these conditions, IMR reflects development.

qa.q: The dependency ratio compares:
qa.a: Under-15s and over-64s with the 15-64 group
qa.e: It measures dependants relative to the working-age population.

qa.q: A town has 2,400 children below 15, 600 people above 64 and 7,500 people aged 15-64. What is the dependency ratio (per 100)?
A demographic dividend can turn into a burden when:
qa.a: Young people lack education and jobs
qa.e: The dividend depends on productive employment of the young.

qa.q: Compared with Uttar Pradesh, Kerala's age pyramid has:
qa.a: A narrower base and more elderly people
qa.e: Low fertility and long life give Kerala an older structure.

qa.q: Population momentum explains why:
qa.a: Population grows for years after fertility falls
qa.e: Many young people entering reproductive ages keep total births high.

qa.q: A pyramid with a wide base and a narrow top indicates:
qa.a: A young population with many children
qa.e: A wide base shows large numbers in the youngest age groups.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): An ageing population can raise the dependency ratio.
Reason (R): People above 64 are counted as dependants.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: More elderly people add to the numerator of the dependency ratio.

qa.q: In India over recent decades, the share of the 0-14 age group has been:
qa.a: Falling
qa.e: Falling fertility shrinks the youngest share while the working-age share grows.

qa.q: Which decade saw negative population growth in India?
qa.e: The influenza epidemic of 1918-19 caused the population to fall.

qa.q: The main cause of negative growth in 1911-21 was:
qa.a: The influenza epidemic of 1918-19
qa.e: Influenza killed millions in 1918-19.

qa.q: India's very rapid population growth during 1951-81 was due mainly to:
qa.a: A sharp fall in the death rate
qa.e: Deaths fell quickly while births stayed high.

qa.q: India's population was about 36 crore in 1951 and about 121 crore in 2011. By how many crore did it increase?
qa.e: Increase = 121 − 36 = 85 crore.

qa.q: Amartya Sen explained famines mainly as a result of:
qa.a: Failure of entitlements to food
qa.e: People starve when they lose the means to buy or produce food.

qa.q: Which was NOT a reason for the fall in death rates in India?
qa.a: Higher age at marriage
qa.e: Age at marriage affects births, not deaths.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): MGNREGA can help prevent famine-like distress.
Reason (R): It gives rural households guaranteed wage work and hence income to buy food.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Guaranteed work protects entitlements, which is exactly Sen's point.

qa.q: India's population in 1901 was about how many crore?
qa.e: It was about 238 million (23.8 crore) in 1901.

qa.q: Why do birth rates usually fall more slowly than death rates?
qa.a: Fertility is shaped by deep-rooted social and cultural norms
qa.e: Values about marriage, children and gender change slowly.

qa.q: Which state reached replacement-level fertility early?
qa.a: Kerala
qa.e: Kerala (and Tamil Nadu) achieved low TFRs early.

qa.q: Which group of states has had relatively high fertility?
qa.a: Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan
qa.e: These north and central states have had higher TFRs.

qa.q: Which factor is most likely to lower fertility?
qa.a: Higher age at marriage for women
qa.e: Later marriage shortens the child-bearing span and reflects women's empowerment.

qa.q: High infant mortality tends to keep birth rates high because:
qa.a: Parents have more children so that some survive
qa.e: When child deaths are common, families compensate with more births.

qa.q: States with high fertility will contribute:
qa.a: A large share of India's future population growth
qa.e: Higher TFR means more births and more growth.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Kerala has low fertility.
Reason (R): Kerala has high female literacy and good health care.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Female literacy and health care are key reasons for Kerala's low TFR.

qa.q: Son preference tends to raise fertility because:
qa.a: Families keep having children until a son is born
qa.e: The wish for a son can push families beyond their intended size.

qa.q: In India the sex ratio is expressed as:
qa.a: Number of females per 1000 males
qa.e: India counts females per 1000 males.

qa.q: India's child sex ratio in 2001 was:
qa.e: It fell from 945 in 1991 to 927 in 2001. (933 was the overall ratio in 2001.)

qa.q: Why is the decline in the child sex ratio especially worrying?
qa.a: It reflects bias against girls at birth and in infancy
qa.e: The 0-6 group captures recent births, so bias here signals sex selection and neglect.

qa.q: Where were some of the lowest child sex ratios found?
qa.a: Prosperous regions like Punjab and Haryana
qa.e: Prosperity did not remove son preference and could even fund sex selection.

qa.q: The PCPNDT Act aims to:
qa.a: Ban the use of techniques to determine a foetus's sex
qa.e: It forbids sex determination to prevent sex-selective abortion.

qa.q: The original PNDT Act was passed in:
qa.e: The PNDT Act came in 1994; it was amended in 2003 and renamed PCPNDT.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Prosperity alone does not improve the sex ratio.
Reason (R): Richer families can more easily afford sex-selective technology.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Wealth can enable sex selection when son preference persists.

qa.q: Which long-term solution does the book stress for improving the sex ratio?
qa.a: A change in social attitudes towards daughters
qa.e: Laws help, but son preference must change for lasting results.

qa.q: India's literacy rate rose from about 18 per cent in 1951 to about what percentage in 2011?
qa.e: Census 2011 recorded literacy of about 74 per cent.

qa.q: Why is female literacy especially important for demography?
qa.a: It is linked to later marriage and lower fertility
qa.e: Educated women tend to marry later, use health care and have fewer children.

qa.q: Which pair shows the regional inequality in literacy?
qa.a: Kerala (very high) and Bihar (much lower)
qa.e: Kerala leads; Bihar has among the lowest literacy rates.

qa.q: Which is a push factor for rural-urban migration?
qa.a: Decline of common property resources
qa.e: Losing village commons pushes people out; the others pull them in.

qa.q: How can urban life benefit people from lower castes?
qa.a: City anonymity can loosen rural caste oppression
qa.e: In the crowd of the city, caste is less visible in daily interaction.

qa.q: About what percentage of Indians lived in rural areas in 2011?
qa.e: Census 2011: about 68.8 per cent rural, 31.2 per cent urban.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Many people still depend on agriculture.
Reason (R): Agriculture's share of India's GDP has risen steadily.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Agriculture's GDP share has fallen even though many still depend on it.

qa.q: Literacy among Scheduled Tribe women is:
qa.a: Lower than the national average
qa.e: Social group and gender inequalities combine to lower ST women's literacy.

qa.q: India launched its national family planning programme in:
qa.e: India's programme began in 1952, among the earliest in the world.

qa.q: The main objective of the family planning programme was to:
qa.a: Influence the rate and pattern of population growth
qa.e: It aimed to shape growth through birth control and health measures.

qa.q: The Emergency period is remembered in population policy for:
qa.a: Coercive mass sterilisation drives
qa.e: Target-driven, forced sterilisation caused a backlash.

qa.q: After the Emergency the programme was renamed:
qa.a: National Family Welfare Programme
qa.e: The new name signalled a shift to welfare and a non-coercive approach.

qa.q: Which goal is shared by the National Population Policy 2000 and the National Health Policy 2017?
qa.a: Reaching replacement-level fertility (TFR 2.1)
qa.e: Both aim at replacement-level TFR and lower infant and maternal mortality.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Coercive methods are an effective long-term solution to population growth.
Reason (R): The Emergency sterilisation drive produced a strong public backlash.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: The backlash shows coercion fails; lasting change follows social and economic development.

qa.q: What is the key lesson of India's population policy experience?
qa.a: Fertility falls with social and economic change, which the state can support
qa.e: The state creates conditions; people's choices change with education and welfare.

qa.q: Which approach best fits today's family welfare programme?
qa.a: Voluntary choice with health counselling
qa.e: Policy now emphasises informed choice and health.

qa.q: The English word 'caste' is derived from:
qa.a: The Portuguese word casta
qa.e: Casta, meaning pure breed, was used by Portuguese observers.

qa.q: The fourfold varna classification consists of:
qa.a: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra
qa.e: These are the four varnas; untouchables were placed outside this scheme.

qa.q: Which statement about jati is correct?
qa.a: Jatis are local groups that vary by region
qa.e: Jatis are numerous, local and regionally variable.

qa.q: Endogamy means:
qa.a: Marrying within one's own caste group
qa.e: Endogamy is marriage inside the group.

qa.q: 'Segmental organisation' of caste refers to:
qa.a: Division of castes into sub-castes
qa.e: Castes are divided into sub-castes and sometimes further.

qa.q: Which is NOT a traditional feature of caste?
qa.a: Membership chosen by the individual
qa.e: Caste membership is fixed at birth.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Caste is an ascribed status.
Reason (R): One is born into one's caste and cannot normally change it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Ascribed status is given at birth, which is exactly how caste works.

qa.q: Historically, caste distinctions were:
qa.a: Less rigid in the early Vedic period than later
qa.e: Caste rigidity increased in the post-Vedic period.

qa.q: The two organising principles of caste are:
qa.a: Separation and hierarchy
qa.e: Castes are kept separate and arranged in a hierarchy.

qa.q: The caste hierarchy is mainly based on the distinction between:
qa.a: Purity and pollution
qa.e: Ritual purity ranks castes higher, pollution lower.

qa.q: Which practice best expresses the principle of separation?
qa.a: Strict rules against marrying outside the caste
qa.e: Endogamy keeps castes separate.

qa.q: The 'wholeness' principle of caste suggests that:
qa.a: Separate castes fit together as ranked parts of one system
qa.e: Like parts of a body, castes have unequal places in the whole.

qa.q: In practice, how were ritual status and economic status related?
qa.a: They usually coincided
qa.e: Upper castes generally also held land and power.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Caste is a system of both difference and inequality.
Reason (R): Castes are separated by rules and ranked by purity and pollution.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The two principles together make caste both divided and unequal.

qa.q: Rules that cooked food may be accepted from some castes but not others are an example of:
qa.a: Both separation and hierarchy
qa.e: Food rules divide groups and rank them by purity.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Upper castes were generally the economically powerful groups in traditional society.
Reason (R): Caste rank and material status tended to coincide.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The coincidence of ritual and material status explains upper-caste economic power.

qa.q: The 1901 census under Herbert Risley was important because it:
qa.a: Tried to record the social hierarchy of castes
qa.e: It attempted to rank castes by social precedence in each region.

qa.q: What was one effect of the attempt to rank castes in the census?
qa.a: Castes petitioned for a higher position
qa.e: Ranking made caste status a matter of competition and official record.

qa.q: Colonial land revenue settlements affected caste by:
qa.a: Giving upper castes legal property rights over land
qa.e: Customary upper-caste rights were recognised as legal ownership.

qa.q: The Government of India Act of 1935 is linked to caste because it:
qa.a: Legally recognised schedules of castes and tribes
qa.e: Lists of castes and tribes for special treatment became 'schedules'.

qa.q: The terms 'Scheduled Castes' and 'Scheduled Tribes' come from:
qa.a: Lists of groups marked for special state treatment
qa.e: The 1935 Act's schedules listed groups for welfare measures.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Colonialism made caste more rigid.
Reason (R): Census enumeration fixed caste identities in official categories.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Fixing fluid identities in records made them more rigid.

qa.q: Which statement best sums up colonialism's impact on caste?
qa.a: It did not invent caste but changed it considerably
qa.e: Caste predates colonialism, but colonial policies reshaped it.

qa.q: Why did colonial rulers try to collect information on caste?
qa.a: To understand and govern Indian society
qa.e: Knowledge of society was seen as necessary for administration.

qa.q: Which group of leaders opposed caste discrimination?
qa.a: Phule, Ambedkar and Gandhi
qa.e: These leaders, in different ways, challenged caste and untouchability.

qa.q: The 'contradiction' in the post-independence state's approach to caste is that it:
qa.a: Sought to abolish caste but used it for reservations
qa.e: To remedy caste injustice, the state had to recognise caste.

qa.q: Which process weakened caste rules in public life?
qa.a: Urbanisation and industrial jobs
qa.e: Mixing in factories, offices and transport made separation hard to keep.

qa.q: In which sphere has caste proved most resilient?
qa.a: Marriage and the home
qa.e: Endogamy remains strong despite public-sphere change.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Most marriages in India still take place within the caste.
Reason (R): Endogamy has weakened as much as caste rules in public life.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Endogamy is the most resilient feature; it has not weakened like public-sphere rules.

qa.q: Why did railways and buses weaken caste rules?
qa.a: People of all castes had to travel together
qa.e: Shared public transport made strict separation impractical.

qa.q: Abolition of caste was part of:
qa.a: The nationalist and reform programme
qa.e: Nationalists and reformers made abolition of caste a goal.

qa.q: Which statement about caste today is most accurate?
qa.a: It has weakened in public life but persists in marriage
qa.e: Change has been uneven across public and private spheres.

qa.q: The concept of 'dominant caste' was developed by:
qa.a: M.N. Srinivas
qa.e: Srinivas used it for numerically large, landowning, powerful castes.

qa.q: A dominant caste is one that is:
qa.a: Numerous, landowning and politically powerful
qa.e: Dominance comes from numbers, land and political power.

qa.q: Which caste is cited in the book as a dominant caste of Karnataka?
qa.a: Vokkaligas
qa.e: Vokkaligas are the example from Karnataka.

qa.q: Many dominant castes rose in power after independence mainly because of:
qa.a: Land reforms that made them owners
qa.e: Land reforms benefited middle castes who became owners.

qa.q: Why has caste become 'invisible' for many urban upper castes?
qa.a: Past caste advantage now passes on as education and wealth
qa.e: Their caste-derived capital no longer needs caste to be visible.

qa.q: For SC, ST and OBC groups, caste has become more visible because:
qa.a: Their claims to state protection depend on caste
qa.e: Reservation and protections are tied to caste identity.

qa.q: 'Vote bank' politics refers to:
qa.a: Parties relying on blocs of community support
qa.e: Caste or community blocs are courted as reliable voters.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Democracy has strengthened caste as a political identity.
Reason (R): Caste associations and parties mobilise voters along caste lines.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Electoral mobilisation gives caste a new political role.

qa.q: 'Tribe' as a category was mainly used for communities that:
qa.a: Lay outside the caste-Hindu social order
qa.e: Tribes were defined in contrast to caste-Hindu society.

qa.q: Which is a 'permanent trait' used to classify tribes?
qa.a: Language
qa.e: Region, language, physical traits and habitat are permanent traits.

qa.q: About what share of India's tribal population lives in 'middle India'?
qa.e: About 85 per cent lives in middle India; over 11 per cent in the North-East.

qa.q: Which language family is spoken entirely by tribal people?
qa.a: Austric
qa.e: Austric speakers are all tribal; over 80 per cent of Tibeto-Burman speakers are tribal.

qa.q: Which tribes are cited as having at least a million members?
qa.a: Gonds, Bhils and Santhals
qa.e: These are among the largest tribes.

qa.q: Tribal people form about what share of India's population?
qa.e: Scheduled Tribes are roughly 8 per cent of the population.

qa.q: Which list gives physical-racial categories once used to classify tribes?
qa.a: Negrito, Australoid, Mongoloid, Dravidian, Aryan
qa.e: These were the racial categories; the other lists are languages, livelihoods and varnas.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Some Indian tribes, such as the Gonds and Bhils, have over a million members.
Reason (R): Tribal people make up about 8 per cent of India's population.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but the national tribal share does not explain why particular tribes are large.

qa.q: Which is an 'acquired trait' used to classify tribes?
qa.a: Mode of livelihood
qa.e: Livelihood and extent of incorporation into Hindu society are acquired traits.

qa.q: Which list correctly gives tribal modes of livelihood?
qa.a: Fishers, hunter-gatherers, shifting cultivators, peasants
qa.e: These are livelihood categories; the others are varna, language and race.

qa.q: The view that tribes are 'secondary' formations means they:
qa.a: Were shaped by long contact with states
qa.e: Their present form grew out of interaction with states and civilisations.

qa.q: Which evidence challenges the idea that tribes were isolated and primitive?
qa.a: Gond kingdoms such as Garha Mandla
qa.e: Tribal kingdoms show state-building and political complexity.

qa.q: In the 1940s, the 'isolationists' argued that tribes:
qa.a: Needed protection from traders, moneylenders and missionaries
qa.e: Protectionists feared exploitation by outsiders.

qa.q: The 'integrationist' view, associated with G.S. Ghurye, held that tribes:
qa.a: Were 'backward Hindus' to be integrated into the mainstream
qa.e: Ghurye stressed links between tribes and Hindu society.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Tribes were never completely isolated from the wider society.
Reason (R): Many tribes traded with, fought for and even formed states.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Trade, military roles and kingdoms prove long contact.

qa.q: Classification of tribes by 'extent of incorporation into Hindu society' is:
qa.a: An acquired trait
qa.e: Incorporation can change over time, so it is acquired.

qa.q: Which statement best describes the impact of national development on tribes?
qa.a: Dams, mines and industries often displaced them
qa.e: Many development projects were sited on tribal land.

qa.q: Which two states were formed in 2000 after long movements with strong tribal participation?
qa.a: Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh
qa.e: Both came out of Bihar and Madhya Pradesh in 2000.

qa.q: The two main issues of tribal movements are:
qa.a: Control over resources and ethnic-cultural identity
qa.e: Land and forests, plus identity, drive tribal movements.

qa.q: How have reservations affected tribal society?
qa.a: They helped create an educated tribal middle class
qa.e: Education and jobs created a middle class active in assertion.

qa.q: In the North-East, special laws limiting civil liberties have been linked to:
qa.a: Cycles of rebellion and repression
qa.e: The book notes a pattern of rebellion and repression.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Tribal identity today is often an assertive identity.
Reason (R): It has been shaped by resistance to forced incorporation into the mainstream.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Resistance to forced incorporation fuels assertion.

qa.q: 'Forced incorporation' of tribes refers to:
qa.a: Being drawn into the mainstream on unfavourable terms
qa.e: Tribes were absorbed into markets and the state with little say.

qa.q: After statehood, which problem continued in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh?
qa.a: Displacement and struggles over resources
qa.e: Mineral wealth kept land and resource conflicts alive.

qa.q: A nuclear family consists of:
qa.a: A couple and their unmarried children
qa.e: That is the definition of the nuclear family.

qa.q: Which statement about Indian families is correct?
qa.a: Nuclear families have always existed in India
qa.e: The 'joint family only' idea is a myth.

qa.q: A matrilocal family is one in which the couple lives with:
qa.a: The wife's parents
qa.e: Matrilocal residence is with the wife's family.

qa.q: Patrilineal means that:
qa.a: Inheritance passes through the father's line
qa.e: Patrilineal refers to descent and succession through males.

qa.q: 'Patriarchal' describes a family in which:
qa.a: Men hold authority and dominate decisions
qa.e: Patriarchy refers to male authority.

qa.q: Which is an example of an 'accidental' change in family structure?
qa.a: Family members separated by war or migration
qa.e: Accidental changes come from events beyond choice.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Grandparents are taking on new roles in many urban families.
Reason (R): With both parents working, grandparents often help with child care.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Dual-earner urban families rely on grandparents for care.

qa.q: Which trend in marriage is noted in the book?
qa.a: More love marriages, though inter-caste unions still face resistance
qa.e: Change is real but uneven; caste still restricts choices.

qa.q: Which communities are examples of matrilineal societies in India?
qa.a: Khasis of Meghalaya and Nairs of Kerala
qa.e: The Khasis and Nairs are the book's examples.

qa.q: Among the Khasis, property passes from:
qa.a: Mother to daughter
qa.e: Khasi inheritance follows the female line.

qa.q: In Khasi society, who controls the property?
qa.a: The mother's brother
qa.e: Control rests with the maternal uncle, not with the woman who inherits.

qa.q: Khasi men experience role strain mainly because:
qa.a: They are torn between natal and conjugal families
qa.e: Duties to sister's household compete with duties to wife and children.

qa.q: The key difference between matriliny and matriarchy is that:
qa.a: Matriliny is about inheritance, matriarchy about authority
qa.e: Inheritance through women is different from women holding power.

qa.q: The book describes matriarchy as:
qa.a: A theoretical idea without clear historical examples
qa.e: No society has been clearly shown to be matriarchal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Khasi society is matrilineal but not matriarchal.
Reason (R): Women inherit property, but men such as maternal uncles hold control.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Inheritance and authority are separated, so matriliny does not equal matriarchy.

qa.q: Son preference in many Indian families is a sign of:
qa.a: Patriarchal norms
qa.e: Valuing sons over daughters reflects patriarchy.

qa.q: According to the chapter, social institutions such as caste and the market:
qa.a: Also produce inequality and exclusion
qa.e: These institutions distribute resources and opportunities unequally.

qa.q: Why do many people believe inequality is natural?
qa.a: It often appears to be deserved or inborn
qa.e: Inequality can look natural, which leads to blaming the poor.

qa.q: 'Blaming the victim' means:
qa.a: Holding the poor responsible for their own poverty
qa.e: It ignores the social causes of disadvantage.

qa.q: Sociology explains most social inequality in terms of:
qa.a: Group-based differences in resources and opportunity
qa.e: Group membership shapes life chances.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Inequality is often social rather than individual.
Reason (R): People's chances are shaped by the groups they are born into.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Birth into caste, class or gender groups shapes opportunities.

qa.q: Which observation best shows that an inequality is social?
qa.a: It repeats across a whole group over time
qa.e: Patterns across groups and generations reveal social inequality.

qa.q: A student interviews a domestic worker and a bank officer about their daily routines. This activity helps to:
qa.a: Reveal structured inequality in everyday life
qa.e: Comparing routines shows how class shapes daily life.

qa.q: Which statement would a sociologist most likely reject?
qa.a: The poor are poor only because they do not work hard
qa.e: This statement blames the victim and ignores social causes.

qa.q: Who identified economic, cultural and social capital?
qa.a: Pierre Bourdieu
qa.e: Bourdieu developed the three forms of capital.

qa.q: Educational qualifications are an example of:
qa.a: Cultural capital
qa.e: Bourdieu classes education and status as cultural capital.

qa.q: Networks of contacts and associations are:
qa.a: Social capital
qa.e: Social capital refers to useful relationships.

qa.q: A wealthy family pays for its son's education at a top college. This shows:
qa.a: Conversion of economic into cultural capital
qa.e: Money (economic) buys education (cultural).

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three senses in which inequality is social?
qa.a: It depends only on individual talent
qa.e: Social inequality goes beyond individual differences.

qa.q: Social inequality is best defined as the unequal distribution of:
qa.a: Socially valued resources like money, education and power
qa.e: It is about valued social resources.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Children of well-connected families often find jobs more easily.
Reason (R): Social capital can be converted into economic advantage.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Contacts (social capital) open doors to jobs (economic capital).

qa.q: How is social inequality different from individual inequality?
qa.a: It is patterned by group membership and structured
qa.e: Social inequality follows group lines systematically.

qa.q: Social stratification refers to:
qa.a: A system ranking categories of people in a hierarchy
qa.e: It is the structured ranking of groups.

qa.q: 'Stratification is a characteristic of society' means that:
qa.a: It is not simply a result of individual differences
qa.e: Stratification is built into society's structure.

qa.q: Which practice helps stratification persist over generations?
qa.a: Inheritance of property and endogamy
qa.e: Passing on resources within closed groups maintains inequality.

qa.q: The idea that caste rank depends on purity and pollution illustrates which principle?
qa.a: Stratification is supported by belief
qa.e: Ideology justifies and supports inequality.

qa.q: 'Life chances' in sociology refers to:
qa.a: Opportunities in health, education and income
qa.e: Life chances depend on one's place in the stratification system.

qa.q: Ascribed status is:
qa.a: Status given at birth, such as caste
qa.e: Ascription is by birth; achievement is by effort.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Stratification tends to persist over generations.
Reason (R): Families pass on resources and status to their children.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Inheritance and family transmission keep stratification going.

qa.q: Why does stratification become more elaborate as societies develop surplus?
qa.a: Surplus creates wealth that can be shared unequally
qa.e: With surplus comes unequal control over it.

qa.q: Prejudice refers to:
qa.a: Pre-formed opinions about a group, not based on evidence
qa.e: Prejudice is an attitude formed in advance of evidence.

qa.q: Prejudice can be:
qa.a: Either positive or negative
qa.e: Prejudice may favour or disfavour a group; both are pre-judgements.

qa.q: The colonial idea of 'martial races' is an example of:
qa.a: A stereotype
qa.e: It assigned a fixed trait to entire communities.

qa.q: Discrimination is best described as:
qa.a: Behaviour that denies a group opportunities
qa.e: Discrimination is action, not just attitude.

qa.q: Why is discrimination often hard to prove?
qa.a: It may be hidden behind reasons such as 'merit'
qa.e: Discriminators rarely state the real reason.

qa.q: A stereotype ignores:
qa.a: Variation among individuals in the group
qa.e: Stereotypes apply a single image to everyone.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Prejudice is resistant to change.
Reason (R): Prejudiced views are often retained even when new evidence contradicts them.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Resistance to evidence is exactly what makes prejudice persist.

qa.q: A student studies how a community is shown in popular films. She is mainly examining:
qa.a: Prejudiced and stereotyped portrayals
qa.e: Media portrayals can carry and spread stereotypes.

qa.q: Social exclusion means:
qa.a: Being cut off from full participation in society
qa.e: It is about denial of participation and access.

qa.q: Social exclusion is described as involuntary because:
qa.a: It happens regardless of the wishes of the excluded
qa.e: The excluded do not choose their exclusion.

qa.q: Which is an example of social exclusion?
qa.a: A group denied access to a public water source
qa.e: Denial of access to common services is exclusion.

qa.q: Why might excluded groups stop trying to take part in society?
qa.a: Repeated rejection discourages them
qa.e: Long exclusion produces withdrawal, which is misread as choice.

qa.q: The 2014 NALSA judgment of the Supreme Court is linked to:
qa.a: Legal recognition of the third gender
qa.e: It recognised transgender persons as a third gender.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Laws against discrimination are necessary but not sufficient.
Reason (R): Prejudice is rooted in social attitudes that law alone cannot change.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Changing attitudes needs social effort beyond law.

qa.q: Which statement about social exclusion is correct?
qa.a: It is structural, not just individual
qa.e: Exclusion is built into social structures.

qa.q: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in:
qa.e: The Act came in 2019, after the 2014 NALSA judgment.

qa.q: According to the ideal model of caste, ritual and economic status were:
qa.a: Supposed to be separate
qa.e: In theory ritual purity was distinct from wealth; in practice they overlapped.

qa.q: In practice, caste and economic status in traditional India:
qa.a: Overlapped strongly
qa.e: Upper castes generally controlled land and wealth.

qa.q: Which social group has the highest proportion of poor people according to the data discussed?
qa.a: Scheduled Tribes
qa.e: STs have the highest poverty, followed by SCs.

qa.q: Since the 19th century, the link between caste and occupation has:
qa.a: Weakened, though caste-class correlation remains
qa.e: Occupations have opened up, but group-level inequality persists.

qa.q: Apartheid in South Africa was:
qa.a: A legal system of racial segregation
qa.e: Apartheid enforced racial separation by law until 1994.

qa.q: Which organisation led the struggle against apartheid?
qa.a: African National Congress
qa.e: The ANC, with Nelson Mandela, led the struggle.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Caste continues to matter for economic inequality.
Reason (R): Poverty rates still follow the caste hierarchy at the group level.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Group-level poverty data show the continuing link.

qa.q: Caste is described as a discriminatory system because it is:
qa.a: Humiliating, exclusionary and exploitative
qa.e: These three aspects describe how caste harms those at the bottom.

qa.q: Untouchability is based on the idea that some castes are:
qa.a: Ritually polluting
qa.e: It stems from the purity-pollution scale.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three dimensions of untouchability?
qa.a: Sanskritisation
qa.e: The three dimensions are exclusion, humiliation-subordination and exploitation.

qa.q: Being forced to perform gestures of deference is an example of:
qa.a: Humiliation-subordination
qa.e: Forced deference humiliates and subordinates.

qa.q: Denial of access to a common water source is an example of:
qa.a: Exclusion
qa.e: Barring access is exclusion.

qa.q: 'Distance pollution' refers to the belief that:
qa.a: Even the presence or shadow of a person could pollute
qa.e: This form was found in parts of southern India.

qa.q: The term 'Dalit' means:
qa.a: Oppressed or downtrodden
